Q2659
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 29-year-old middle-eastern man presents with bilateral painful red eyes, photophobia, and decreased vision. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes a small hypopyon in the right eye. What is the most common systemic finding associated with this patient’s condition?
Correct answer: D. aphthous ulcers
Rationale
Behçet disease (BD) may present as bilateral anterior uveitis, and can have an associated hypopyon. Anterior uveitis may be the only ocular manifestation of BD; it presents with a transient hypopyon in up to 25% of cases. Aphthous ulcers are the most common systemic manifestation of Behçet disease. These are recurrent mucosal ulcers that produce significant discomfort and pain. They can occur on the lips, gums, palate, tongue, uvula, and posterior pharynx. They are discrete, round or oval, white ulcerations with red rims that vary in size from 2 to 15 mm. They recur every 5-10 days or every month. They last from 7 to 10 days and then heal without much scarring unless they are large. Vitiligo is a finding that may be associated with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, and is not a finding in Behçet disease. Gastrointestinal ulcers are included in the minor diagnostic criteria of Behçet disease, but are not the most common systemic finding. Paresthesias may be present in patients with multiple sclerosis who have intermediate uveitis. They are not a common finding in Behçet disease.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2660
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What subset of lymphocytes is thought to play a major role in fighting parasitic infections?
Correct answer: C. Th2 lymphocytes
Rationale
Th2 lymphocytes are thought to play a major role in parasitic infections (as well as late-phase response of allergic reactions, asthma and atopic disease).
Th1 lymphocytes are thought to play a major role in the classic delayed hypersensitivity reaction (eg, purified protein derivative [PPD] skin reaction), immunity to intracellular infections, immunity to fungi, most forms of severe T lymphocyte-mediated autoimmune disease, and chronic transplant rejection.
Cytotoxic T lymphocytes are especially good at killing tumor and virus-infected cells.
Natural killer (NK) cells are a subset of non-T, non-B lymphocytes that also kill tumor-and virus-infected cells, but unlike cytotoxic T lymphocytes, NK cells do not have a specific antigen receptor.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2661
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What test commonly gives a false-positive result in patients with leptospirosis?
Correct answer: A. fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-Abs)
Rationale
False positives with the purified protein derivative (PPD) can occur in a patient who has had a prior bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination, atypical mycobacterial infections, and bladder cancer.
Interferon gamma release assays (IGRAs) are much less frequently associated with false positives compared to PPD in the setting of prior BCG vaccination. Urine histoplasmin antigen testing is carried out when there is suspicion for Histoplasma capsulatum infection. False positives are rare. False positives with the FTA-Abs are not uncommon in certain settings, which is why a thorough review of systems and history is vital. False positives with the FTA-Abs occur in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), tuberculosis, HIV, pregnancy, malaria, recent vaccination, and spirochetal infections. Other spirochetes beside Treponema pallidum include Borrelia burgdorferi and Leptospira species.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2662
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What should be the first mode of therapy in sarcoid-associated retinal and optic disc neovascularization?
Correct answer: A. corticosteroid or immunomodulatory therapy
Rationale
The presence of uveitic retinal neovascularization does not always require panretinal photocoagulation. Some cases of sarcoid panuveitis can present with neovascularization of the disc that resolves completely with systemic immunomodulatory and corticosteroid therapy alone.
If there is angiographic evidence of ischemia, as can be the case with retinal vasculitis or Eales disease, then scatter laser photocoagulation or intravitreal anti-VEGF injection may be recommended.
Although an inferior transseptal approach is a technique for periocular steroid administration, it is not necessarily indicated in sarcoid-related retinal and optic disc neovascularization.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2663
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
The major criteria of diagnosing Behçet disease (BD) include oral ulceration and what other finding?
Correct answer: D. uveitis or retinal vasculitis
Rationale
The diagnosis of BD is based entirely on clinical findings. The diagnostic criteria, according to the International Study Group for Behçet's disease, include recurrent oral and genital ulcers, ocular inflammation, skin lesions, and a positive cutaneous pathergy test.
Although arthritis, as well as cardiac, gastrointestinal, pulmonary, and central nervous system (CNS) involvement, have been reported in patients with Behçet disease, these are not major criteria for diagnosis. Conversely, BD may have its predominant effect on a single system; special clinical types may occur: neuro-BD, ocular BD, intestinal BD.
There are no laboratory tests that are specific for the disease. Patients may have elevated inflammatory markers such as the sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, but these are not useful in making a diagnosis. HLA-B51 testing has been associated to some extent with ocular lesions in certain populations, but it is of little diagnostic value.

Q2664
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What risk factor in a patient with West Nile virus (WNV)-associated uveitis is associated with an increased risk of WNV-associated mortality?
Correct answer: C. diabetes mellitus
Rationale
Diabetes mellitus and advanced age in someone with West Nile virus (WNV)-associated uveitis are associated with the development of severe neurologic disease (meningitis or encephalitis). In addition, diabetes mellitus has been implicated as a risk factor for WNV-related death. Systemically, a patient may present with fever, myalgias, headache, conjunctivitis, and a maculopapular rash. Cardiomyopathy has not been associated with an increased risk of WNV-associated mortality.

Q2665
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common presentation of uveitis caused by tuberculosis (TB)?
Correct answer: A. disseminated choroiditis
Rationale
Disseminated choroiditis is the most common presentation of ocular tuberculosis. This manifests as multiple deep, yellowish lesions, or tubercles, in the posterior pole that may be accompanied by disc edema, anterior uveitis, or vitritis. Isolated granulomatous anterior uveitis secondary to TB is very rare. Iris nodules may be seen in TB but are less common than choroiditis. Retinal perivasculitis is more commonly seen in Eales disease. Retinal involvement in TB is usually secondary to extension of choroidal disease.

Q2666
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
In a 53-year-old woman with peripapillary atrophy and punched-out chorioretinal scars (histo spots), what is the most likely cause of her recent decrease in visual acuity?
Correct answer: B. macular choroidal neovascularization
Rationale
Peripapillary atrophy, multiple atrophic punched-out chorioretinal scars (histo spots), and choroidal neovascular membrane causing maculopathy in the absence of vitreous cells constitute the clinical triad for the diagnosis of ocular histoplasmosis syndrome. Acute reduction in central vision typically indicates macular involvement with choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in such eyes. If histo spots are seen in the macula, there is a 25% chance of macular CNV developing in 3 years. If no spots are observed, the chances are 2%. In the later stages, when neovascular membranes are typically seen, vitritis is uncommon. Optic neuropathy is not a typical manifestation of ocular histoplasmosis, and a macular scar would not be expected to cause a new deterioration in vision.

Q2667
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What test is useful in the diagnosis of tubular interstitial nephritis and uveitis?
Correct answer: B. urine ß2-microglobulin level
Rationale
An increased urine level of β2-microglobulin is a useful marker for tubular interstitial nephritis and uveitis (TINU). Patients with TINU can also test positive for antinuclear antibody and have an elevated sedimentation rate, but these findings are not always present and are not specific. Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level has not been reported with TINU. Patients with TINU can also have hematuria and proteinuria along with elevated serum creatinine level, eosinophilia, and slightly abnormal results on liver function tests.

Q2668
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 70-year-old woman has chronic anterior uveitis that responds poorly when treated with topical prednisolone acetate, 1%. The examination reveals extensive fibrin formation and posterior synechiae that prevent view of the posterior segment. On gonioscopy, a pigmented mass is seen in the angle from 10 to 1 o'clock. What is the next step?
Correct answer: A. Obtain a B-scan.
Rationale
Melanomas can be associated with an impressive inflammatory response, and ciliary body melanomas can break through to the anterior segment. The differential diagnosis includes infections, chronic retinal detachment, and metastatic tumors. In the absence of a posterior segment view, B-scan ultrasonography and, when available, ultrasound biomicroscopy or anterior segment optical coherence tomography, can be very helpful.

Q2669
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What finding is most likely in an eye with Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHIC; also called Fuchs uveitis syndrome or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) in the absence of prior surgery?
Correct answer: B. diffuse stellate keratoprecipitates (KP)
Rationale
Diffuse stellate keratoprecipitates are typically seen in FHIC and do not follow the pattern of the Arlt triangle, but are rather diffusely spread over the endothelial surface (similar to many other viral uveitides; there is data in the literature that now suggests FHIC is likely to be Rubella-associated anterior uveitis, which would place FHIC in the viral uveitides category). The diffuse stellate KP of FHIC are not symptomatic and should not be treated with corticosteroids, as not only do they not respond to treatment, but corticosteroids will only raise the risk of cataract formation and a steroid-induced pressure response. Patients with FHIC are not at risk for acute pressure spikes, but are at risk for the development of chronic, secondary open-angle glaucoma (along with cataracts and floaters) and should be followed as glaucoma suspects.
Patients with FHIC typically do not present with CME, especially in the absence of prior surgery.
While patients with FHIC can form posterior synechiae AFTER cataract surgery, the question specifically asks about the presence of posterior synechiae PRIOR to surgery, which patients with FHIC do not have.
Iris nodules are associated with granulomatous uveitides. FHIC does not usually present as a granulomatous uveitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2670
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What medicine can be given intravitreally to treat ocular toxoplasmosis in patients who are intolerant to systemic therapy?
Correct answer: B. clindamycin
Rationale
Ocular toxoplasmosis is usually treated with oral antibiotics. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is most commonly used. Triple therapy with sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, and prednisone, or quadruple therapy, with the addition of clindamycin, may also be used. In patients who are intolerant to systemic therapy or fail to respond to systemic therapy, intravitreal clindamycin can be used with or without dexamethasone. Intravitreal amikacin and vancomycin are used to treat bacterial endophthalmitis. Intravitreal voriconazole is used to treat fungal endophthalmitis.

Q2671
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is a characteristic feature seen on gonioscopy of Fuchs uveitis syndrome?
Correct answer: B. abnormal blood vessels bridging the angle that may bleed during surgery
Rationale
Fuchs uveitis syndrome (sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is unilateral, and symptoms range from none to mild blurring and discomfort. Signs include diffuse stromal atrophy with a "moth-eaten appearance" of the iris; small white stellate keratic precipitates scattered diffusely over the endothelium; anterior chamber cell; no synechiae; and abnormal vessels bridging the angle on gonioscopy that may bleed during surgery, causing a hyphema, glaucoma, and cataract. Few cases require treatment of the inflammation, and macular edema is uncommon. Histological examination shows plasma cells in the ciliary body. The etiology remains unclear but has been associated with rubella, toxoplasmosis, and cytomegalovirus.

Q2672
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For patients requiring long-term uveitis therapy, noncorticosteroid, immunosuppressive agents should be considered if the total daily dose of prednisone cannot be maintained in what dosage range?
Correct answer: A. 7.5 mg or less
Rationale
The prednisone dosage must be maintained at 7.5 mg or less per day. A higher dosage of corticosteroids required for more than 3 months places the patient at risk for corticosteroid-induced side effects and warrants initiation of other immunomodulators as steroid-sparing agents.

What endogenous fungal infection is the most common cause of endophthalmitis?
Correct answer: A. Candida
Rationale
Candida

Candida species are the most common fungal cause of endogenous endophthalmitis.

Q2674
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Among patients who are seropositive for human immunodeficiency virus, what change has most likely contributed to the decrease in the incidence of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis?
Correct answer: A. highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART)
Rationale
With the introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy, the incidence of CMV retinitis decreased by 80%. HAART helps many patients maintain higher CD4 counts, decreasing the incidence of many of the opportunistic infections seen at lower CD4 levels; this explains most of the decrease in cases of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis among patients infected with human immunodeficiency virus. Prophylactic antivirals are not routinely used for CMV, given the cost and potential side effects (including myelosuppression) of the only effective oral agent, valganciclovir. Once a patient is diagnosed with CMV retinitis, however, they may remain on valganciclovir indefinitely or until the CD4 count recovers. Ganciclovir implants are very effective in controlling CMV retinitis when it occurs but are not used to prevent primary retinitis. Routine screening protocols are still recommended, but this does not prevent CMV retinitis.

Q2675
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Mast cells bind which immunoglobulin (Ig) type to their cell surfaces?
Correct answer: A. IgE
Rationale
Immunoglobulin E (IgE) binds to the surface of mast cells and participates in allergic reactions. IgM and IgG are involved in the initial and memory responses of the immune arc, respectively. IgA is primarily involved in mucosal immunity.

Q2676
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient with bilateral pars planitis who is being treated with mycophenolate mofetil exhibits recurrent uveitic macular edema (UME) in the right eye. The anterior chamber and vitreous are inactive with respect to inflammation in both eyes, yet the macular edema persists. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula demonstrates uveitic macular edema in the right eye, but the OCT image is otherwise unremarkable. What is the best initial choice in managing the macular edema in this patient?
Correct answer: C. periocular sub-Tenon injection of triamcinolone
Rationale
Uveitic macular edema is a frequent complication of uveitis and may occur even when inflammation is otherwise controlled. Optical coherence tomography of the macula can help identify contributing factors to the macular edema, such as vitreomacular traction. If there is prominent vitreomacular traction, a pars plana vitrectomy may be considered. In this case, however, although there is uveitic macular edema, the imaging is otherwise unremarkable. If there were persistently active intraocular inflammation that may be driving the uveitic macular edema, advancing a patient’s systemic therapy may be beneficial. However, this patient’s intraocular inflammation is inactive. In addition, advancing therapy from an antimetabolite (mycophenolate mofetil) to an alkylating agent (cyclophosphamide) is not indicated, because alkylating agents are reserved for aggressive, sight-threatening causes of ocular inflammation due to their significant side effects. Similarly, intravenous methylprednisolone would not be indicated as the first step in managing this patient’s macular edema, although such therapy can be used initially for robust intraocular inflammation that must be managed quickly and requires doses higher than what may be needed with oral corticosteroids. The use of periocular sub-Tenon triamcinolone, then, is the best initial choice in managing this patient’s uveitic macular edema.
The injections may be repeated monthly. If UME persists, then 2–4 mg of intravitreal preservative-free triamcinolone may be considered. Intravitreal triamcinolone can be highly effective in reducing UME, particularly in non-vitrectomized eyes, but its effect is time limited; the drug is eliminated more quickly from the vitreous cavity of vitrectomized eyes.
Sustained delivery of corticosteroid to the vitreous cavity through the use of implants is also effective.

Q2677
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
In a patient with uveitis and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), what mechanism of increased IOP is most likely to be reversed with aggressive use of corticosteroids?
Correct answer: D. anterior rotation of ciliary body due to shallow choroidal effusions
Rationale
Of the answer choices provided, resolution of inflammatory anterior choroidal effusions in the setting of corticosteroid therapy will often result in posterior rotation of the ciliary body (CB) back to its native state, relieving the patient of secondary angle closure. (Another scenario where corticosteroid therapy in the setting of uveitis and elevated IOP can help lower the IOP is when there is an associated "trabeculitis," oftentimes seen in viral anterior uveitides).
Of course, cycloplegics should also be used when anterior rotation of the ciliary body is thought to be a cause of increased IOP.
Elevated IOP due to synechial angle closure will not respond to corticosteroid therapy, nor will a steroid response (in fact, it will only get worse with continued corticosteroids).
Decreased aqueous production by the CB is one of the reasons patients with uveitis tend to have lower-than-baseline IOPs; treatment with corticosteroids causes resolution of intraocular inflammation and typically results in elevation of IOP back to baseline in these patients.

Q2678
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
In a patient with multifocal choroiditis, what is the preferred management of chronic inflammation?
Correct answer: A. immunomodulatory therapy
Rationale
Multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis is an idiopathic inflammatory disorder of choroid, retina, and vitreous. It is more common in young, myopic women. It presents with photopsias, enlarged physiologic blind spot, and decreased vision. Because this is a chronic, recurrent inflammatory disease, immunomodulatory therapy with steroids or steroid-sparing agents is recommended.
A viral etiology with herpes simplex and Epstein-Barr virus has been suggested but not verified; antiviral therapy is not used.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs are important adjuncts for the treatment of CNV. There is no role of cryotherapy.

Q2679
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For a patient with uveitis complicated by glaucoma, what glaucoma surgery has the highest likelihood of increasing inflammation in the perioperative period?
Correct answer: D. endoscopic laser cyclophotocoagulation
Rationale
Any intraocular procedure can be associated with increased inflammation, especially in eyes with uveitis or an otherwise altered blood-ocular barrier. However, cyclodestructive procedures such as cyclophotocoagulation have a higher risk of worsening inflammation and leading to hypotony and phthisis bulbi.

Q2680
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 32-year-old woman presents with photophobia and blurred vision. Examination shows a granulomatous anterior uveitis with vitritis and macular edema. What panel of laboratory tests would be appropriate to establish the diagnosis of sarcoidosis?
Correct answer: C. chest x-ray, serum lysozyme, conjunctival biopsy
Rationale
Sarcoidosis is a protean disease that can affect any bodily tissue. However, it most commonly affects the lungs, skin, and eyes. In addition to the granulomatous uveitis, sarcoidosis can involve any ocular tissue as a granulomatous uveitis or vasculitis. The workup involves screening the tissues most commonly affected by sarcoidosis, including the lungs (chest x-ray or CT scan, serum lysozyme test, angiotensin-converting enzyme [ACE] test). Conjunctival biopsies have been shown to be positive when directed to a probable granuloma and in asymptomatic conjunctiva.
Other tests that may be useful include a gallium scan, an angiotensin-converting enzyme test, a chest CT, and a lacrimal gland biopsy. However, an aqueous tap for PCR would not be useful for confirming sarcoidosis, but it would be helpful if evaluating a retinal vasculitis or retinitis, especially if a viral cause were suspected. A retinal biopsy and RPR would be useful for evaluating an unexplained retinitis due to virus or syphilis. HLA typing is unhelpful for evaluation of sarcoidosis.

Q2681
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What biologic immunomodulatory agent has an approved indication for treating noninfectious posterior uveitis?
Correct answer: C. adalimumab
Rationale
Adalimumab, a fully human biologic monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 directed against tumor necrosis factor alpha, is the first immunomodulatory therapy to be approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for treating uveitis (noninfectious posterior uveitis). Infliximab is a mouse-human chimeric G1 immunoglobulin that similarly targets tumor necrosis factor alpha. Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody directed against CD20+ cells, and can be used to target B lymphocytes. Etanercept is another biologic agent that targets TNF-alpha, although it is ineffective against treating uveitis, and paradoxically is associated with development of an inflammatory syndrome similar to sarcoidosis in some cases.

Q2682
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 75-year-old man is having trouble driving at night and reading small print. He sees intermittent flashes of light OU. Visual acuity is 20/50 OD, 20/20 OS with no relative afferent pupillary defect. There is 2+ nuclear sclerosis OU. The fundus appearance and optical coherence tomography (OCT) result are shown in the figure. What testing and/or management should be pursued at this time?
Correct answer: C. full-field electroretinography
Rationale
This patient notes photopsias and night blindness. The fundus examination shows severe vascular attenuation without obvious pigmentary changes. The OCT shows hyperreflectivity and disruption of the outer nuclear layer and decreased reflectivity in the ellipsoid zone. This constellation of symptoms and findings in a 75-year-old patient raises concern for a paraneoplastic process such as cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR).
A full-field electroretinogram (ERG) will be abnormal in CAR. The characteristic ERG in CAR shows decreased cone responses. Blood tests for anti-retinal antibodies also can be obtained, although the antibodies often are nonspecific. MRI of the brain/orbits is not indicated, given the lack of evidence for optic nerve disease or other central nervous system disease. Observation is not appropriate in this situation, given the funduscopic and OCT findings, and cataract surgery should not be done until alternative causes for the vision loss are excluded.

Q2683
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
An individual infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) has necrotizing retinitis. What test would be most helpful in making the diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. anterior chamber tap for polymerase chain reaction
Rationale
Necrotizing retinitis in patients with HIV can be caused by herpes viruses (varicella zoster virus [VZV], cytomegalovirus [CMV], herpes simplex virus [HSV]). The diagnosis is made clinically, but intraocular fluid analysis of aqueous or vitreous samples or retinal biopsy should be performed. Intraocular antibody production can be computed using Goldmann-Witmer (GW) coefficient. Polymerase chain reaction is the most sensitive, specific, and rapid mode of diagnosis for early initiation of appropriate therapy.
Serum and urine testing for these agents may be contributory but not diagnostic of ocular infection.

Q2684
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the pathogen associated with the development of Kaposi sarcoma?
Correct answer: D. human herpesvirus 8
Rationale
The pathogen involved with the development of Kaposi sarcoma is human herpesvirus (HHV)-8. HHV-4 is also known as Epstein-Barr virus and is associated with the development of primary central nervous system lymphomas and primary vitreoretinal lymphomas in HIV-infected individuals. Herpes simplex virus type 1 and cytomegalovirus (HHV-5) are not associated with any specific neoplasias in HIV.

Q2685
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient is suspected to have Propionibacterium acnes endophthalmitis after cataract surgery. What antibiotic is recommended for vitreous injection?
Correct answer: C. vancomycin
Rationale
The intravitreal or endocapsular antibiotic that is appropriate for the treatment of P acnes (a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus) is vancomycin. P acnes endophthalmitis often presents with mild inflammation postoperatively, and the hallmark feature is a whitish intracapsular plaque (or plaques). Suspicion can be confirmed with Gram stain and/or anaerobic cultures, which should be held for at least 2 weeks because P acnes is a slow-growing organism. Although intravitreal or endocapsular injection of vancomycin may initially help, inflammation frequently recurs, and curative therapy often requires vitrectomy, with or without capsulectomy and with or without intraocular lens (IOL) removal.

Q2686
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Indocyanine green angiography is most likely to be clinically useful for what vascular abnormality?
Correct answer: C. choroidal neovascularization or inflammation blocked by pigment or blood
Rationale
Indocyanine green angiography (ICG) provides better visualization of the choroid than the retina. ICG molecules tend not to extravasate from the choroidal circulation as do those of the fluorescein. The light scatter with ICG angiography is much less than with fluorescein, so ICG is more helpful when ocular media is hazy or there is overlying pigment or blood.
Racemose hemangiomas, which are retinal arteriovenous communications without interposed capillaries, intraretinal microvascular abnormality (IRMA), and retinal ischemia, are best diagnosed and assessed by fundus fluorescein angiogram.

Q2687
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Over the last 3 months, a 53-year-old woman has developed occasional headaches and intermittent left eye pain and blurring. Her only medication is oral doxycycline for rosacea. Her visual acuity is 20/20 on the right and 20/40 on the left, and her color vision, pupillary reactions, and slit-lamp examination are normal OU. She has metamorphopsia on Amsler grid testing in the left eye. Given her fundus appearance shown, what is her most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. scleritis
Rationale
This patient has horizontal choroidal folds in the left eye from posterior scleritis, which may cause intermittent eye pain with choroidal folds. Demyelinating optic neuritis is not associated with choroidal folds. The absence of optic disc edema and the prolonged painful course excludes anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Toxic optic neuropathy is bilateral and associated with progressive optic disc pallor, and not choroidal folds.

Q2688
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is a major risk factor for the development of primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) and primary intraocular lymphoma?
Correct answer: D. immunosuppression
Rationale
The most significant risk factor for the development of primary intraocular lymphoma and primary CNS lymphomas is immunodeficiency. This includes HIV infection (which increases the risk from 50- to 500-fold), iatrogenic immune suppression, and aging (half of all cases occur after 60 years of age).
The incidence of PCNSL appears to be increasing and is projected to occur in 1 of every 100,000 immunocompetent patients.

Q2689
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What condition should be considered in a 62-year-old patient presenting with a vitreous full of cells and no focal fundus lesions?
Correct answer: C. intraocular lymphoma
Rationale
All of the conditions listed can produce varying degrees of vitritis, with associated floaters and a decrease in vision. However, birdshot retinochoroidopathy and MEWDS more typically present with more prominent retinal/subretinal lesions with mild to minimal vitritis, whereas MS typically presents with optic neuritis and extremity paresthesia/weakness.
In a 62-year-old patient with no prior history of uveitis (in fact, in any patient over 45 without any prior history of uveitis) who presents with a first-time episode of vitritis, intraocular lymphoma must be considered and ruled out. Intraocular lymphoma can also include deep, choroidal, yellowish infiltrates similar to those seen in white-dot syndromes, but again, vitritis in an older individual without prior history of uveitis must be investigated for intraocular lymphoma.

Q2690
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What clinical feature of multifocal choroiditis is helpful in differentiating it from ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS)?
Correct answer: A. vitritis
Rationale
Multifocal choroiditis is associated with varying degrees of vitritis, which distinguishes it from ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS).
Choroidal neovascular membrane, bilateral involvement, and punched-out scars are seen in OHS and multifocal choroiditis.

Q2691
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient with a mature, white cataract develops anterior chamber inflammation and an elevated IOP. If the lens capsule has not been penetrated or traumatized, what is the most likely mechanism of inflammation and increased pressure?
Correct answer: D. clogging of the trabecular meshwork by macrophages engorged with lens proteins
Rationale
Phacolytic glaucoma and uveitis is the result of lens protein leaking through an intact capsule, typically in a hypermature cataract. Macrophages scavenge the protein from the anterior chamber, occlude the trabecular meshwork, and result in an elevated IOP. Delamination of the lens capsule is a feature of exfoliation syndrome, not phacolytic uveitis. Zonal granulomas are a histopathological inflammatory finding in a disrupted or traumatized lens, surrounding the site of capsule injury; in contrast, in cases of phacolytic glaucoma the capsule is presumably intact.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2692
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What type of lymphocytes participate in the innate immune response?
Correct answer: C. natural killer cells and intraepithelial lymphocytes
Rationale
Lymphocytes include B cells, T cells, and non-B, non-T lymphocytes. Two types of lymphocytes participate in the innate immune response: 1) gamma-delta (γδ) T cells or sentinel T cells, also known as intraepithelial lymphocytes, and 2) natural killer cells. These serve as a bridge between innate and adaptive responses.
Eosinophils are important in allergic immune reactions and parasitic infections. Basophils are the blood-borne equivalent of tissue-bound mast cells, which act as major effector cells in IgE-mediated inflammatory reactions. Langerhans cells are myeloid cells with dendritic cell function.

Q2693
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is a typical finding of primary central nervous system (CNS)/intraocular lymphoma?
Correct answer: A. multifocal, retinal, and subretinal pigment epithelial (sub-RPE) infiltrates
Rationale
The most typical findings for primary vitreoretinal (intraocular) lymphoma, which is a subset of primary CNS lymphoma, are creamy yellowish/whitish subretinal and sub-RPE infiltrates and vitritis. Although anterior chamber cells and, rarely, pseudohypopyon can be seen, such findings are much less common than the vitreous and posterior segment findings. Instead, intense anterior chamber cell reaction with hypopyon can be seen in endophthalmitis, HLA-B27 positive seronegative spondyloarthropathy-associated recurrent anterior uveitis, and Behçet disease.
Pars plana exudates (snowbanking) can occasionally be seen in intraocular lymphoma, but more frequently in pars planitis and intermediate uveitis related to sarcoidosis. Extensive vasculitis involving primarily the venules is a feature of sarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis, and tuberculosis.

What uveitic condition is (weakly) associated with HLA-DR4?
Correct answer: A. sympathetic ophthalmia
Rationale
HLA-DR4 has been weakly associated with both Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome and sympathetic ophthalmia.

Q2695
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What type of  juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is associated with the highest risk for uveitis?
Correct answer: C. oligoarticular onset
Rationale
Anterior uveitis can be associated with all forms of JIA. Oligoarticular onset (previously known as pauciarticular onset) JIA accounts for 80%-90% of patients with JIA-associated uveitis. Four or fewer joints are involved during the first 6 months of disease. The severity, onset, and exacerbations of uveitis can be different from the joint disease; that is, severe anterior uveitis can occur with mild arthritis as well as before or after the arthritis. Nevertheless, it should be noted that no matter how severe the anterior uveitis, it is asymptomatic in nature, and therefore it is crucial for children diagnosed with JIA to be screened for ocular involvement.

Q2696
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What pathologic finding characterizes lens-induced uveitis after trauma?
Correct answer: C. granulomatous inflammation around the lens
Rationale
Histologically, a zonal granulomatous inflammation is found at the site of lens injury. Neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, epithelioid cells, and giant cells may be seen.
Uveitis may result from an immune reaction to lens material. This may occur after trauma or surgery associated with disruption of the lens capsule or from leakage of lens proteins through the lens capsule in mature or hypermature cataracts (phacolysis). Specifically, phacolytic uveitis (or phacolytic glaucoma, as it is frequently termed) involves an acute increase in intraocular pressure (IOP) caused by clogging of the trabecular meshwork by macrophages engorged with lens proteins leaking through the intact capsule of a hypermature cataract.
Juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG) is a benign proliferative disorder of histiocytic cells of the dermal dendrocyte phenotype. JXG belongs to the broad group of non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses and is typically a disorder of early childhood. JXG presents in the first 2 years of life as a solitary reddish or yellowish skin papule or nodule. Ocular lesions can involve the eyelids or iris. Histologically, JXG is characterized by the presence of foamy or Touton giant cells.
Asteroid bodies are star-shaped, acidophilic bodies found within the multinucleated giant cells of sarcoidosis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2697
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A myopic male patient with a history of lattice degeneration presents with mild distortion of the vision in the right eye for 2 weeks. On examination there are 1+ anterior chamber and vitreous cells, including pigment granules in the eye. The intraocular pressure (IOP) is 28. There are no keratic precipitates or posterior synechiae. There is a peripheral retinal detachment in the right eye, with what appears to be a flap tear. Examination of the left eye reveals no pathology. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. Schwartz syndrome
Rationale
This patient has all the risk factors for retinal detachment; he is myopic and has lattice degeneration.
Peripheral retinal detachment can be associated with anterior segment inflammation without posterior synechiae and vitreous inflammation with pigmentary cells (Schwartz syndrome). The anterior chamber cells are photoreceptor outer segments liberated from the subretinal space. These photoreceptor outer segments are phagocytosed by the endothelial cells of the trabecular meshwork and cause elevation of the intraocular pressure.
Behçet disease is a chronic, relapsing, multisystem inflammatory disorder of unknown etiology that can affect both the anterior and the posterior segments of the eye, often simultaneously. Sites of ocular involvement in primary vitreoretinal lymphoma can include the vitreous, retina, subretinal pigment epithelium, and any combination thereof. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome is a multisystem disease of presumed autoimmune etiology that is characterized by chronic, bilateral, diffuse, granulomatous panuveitis with accompanying integumentary, neurologic, and auditory involvement.

Q2698
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Abnormal urinalysis findings, with increased ß2-microglobulin level, in a patient with uveitis should prompt initiation of what systemic treatment?
Correct answer: A. steroids
Rationale
Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis (TINU) syndrome occurs in adolescent girls and women. The mean age of onset is 21 years. Uveitis is typically a bilateral, nongranulomatous, anterior uveitis. Posterior segment involvement is rare but may include vitritis, multifocal chorioretinal lesions, and retinal vascular leakage, as well as optic nerve edema and macular edema. More commonly, patients may present with systemic symptoms before the development of uveitis. These patients may have abnormal serum creatinine level or decreased creatinine clearance; abnormal urinalysis findings, with increased ß2-microglobulin level, proteinuria, presence of eosinophils, pyuria or hematuria, urinary white cell casts, and normoglycemic glycosuria. TINU syndrome is responsive to high-dose oral corticosteroids. A small proportion of patients with a prolonged course may require immunomodulatory therapy.

Q2699
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 25-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of vision loss in the right eye. He states that he is HIV positive, with a CD4+ count of 44 cells/μL. His visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye and count fingers at 3 feet in the right eye. The examination of the left eye is unremarkable. Fundus examination of the right eye is shown in the figure. What is the most appropriate initial management of this patient's condition?
Correct answer: D. intravenous ganciclovir
Rationale
The figure depicts cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis in an HIV-positive patient. CMV retinitis is the most common ocular opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS (and is an AIDS-defining illness). However, over the past 2 decades since the introduction of modern antiretroviral therapy, the prevalence of CMV retinitis has decreased dramatically. CMV retinitis usually occurs when CD4+ count drops below 50 cells/μL. Patients present with blurry vision and/or floaters. Clinically, the retina appears white and may have intraretinal hemorrhage, exudate, necrosis, periphlebitis, or "frosted-branch" angiitis. Vitritis may or may not be present, and when present it is usually mild. Retinal detachment occurs in up to half of the patients. Laser photocoagulation and pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade are frequently used to try to control or prevent retinal detachment, with variable success.
Options for systemic coverage include high-dose induction with either intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg twice daily) or foscarnet (90 mg/kg twice daily) for 2 weeks, followed by low-dose daily maintenance therapy or oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily) for 3 weeks, followed by maintenance therapy (900 mg/day). Then patients may be switched to oral ganciclovir if they clinically improve. If patients do not improve, a ganciclovir intravitreal implant can be used. Oral valganciclovir 900 mg twice per day for 3 weeks is another acceptable induction therapy, if intravenous therapy is not desired. Intravitreal ganciclovir and foscarnet have been used off-label as well. Myelosuppression is a known side effect of systemic ganciclovir.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2700
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A young, otherwise healthy man presents to the emergency department with sudden central vision loss in one eye that occurred a couple of days previously. He now reports seeing flashes of light and has subsequent vision loss in the other eye. His fundus examination and fluorescein angiography are shown in the figures. What life-threatening condition is associated with the ocular condition he likely has?
Correct answer: A. cerebral vasculitis
Rationale
First, one must realize that the patient has acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE), which is a white dot syndrome or inflammatory chorioretinopathy that is diagnosed by clinical presentation and fluorescein angiography findings in the early phase of the disease. It presents like the case in the question stem, with sudden unilateral vision loss with central and paracentral scotomas, and involvement of the fellow eye within days to weeks. Photopsias may precede vision loss. As seen in the fundus photo, APMPPE is characterized by multiple scattered large (1-2 disc areas), flat, yellow-white placoid lesions in the posterior pole, at the retinal pigment epithelium level, with minimal anterior segment inflammation and possible mild vitritis. Fluorescein angiography (FA) shows early hypofluorescent lesions (either corresponding to or more numerous than the lesions seen on funduscopy), and late hyperfluorescent staining, as seen in the FA in the question. When neurologic symptoms are present in the setting of the above findings, then cerebral vasculitis must be ruled out with full neurologic evaluation, as it is a life-threatening entity associated with APMPPE. Out of the white dot syndromes, only APMPPE is associated with cerebral vasculitis. The other posterior uveitides associated with cerebral vasculitis are collagen vascular diseases such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Visual prognosis in APMPPE is favorable in that most patients regain 20/40 or better vision within 6 months. Residual visual dysfunction can occur in about 20% of patients. While systemic corticosteroids are not definitively beneficial for visual outcomes, they are indicated for patients with CNS vasculitis.
Focal segmental glomerulonephritis (FSGS) is incorrect; it is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). GPA is a collagen vascular disease associated with anterior, intermediate, and posterior uveitis in  ~10% of patients, with retinitis reported in up to 20% of patients. The retinitis presents as cotton-wool spots (Fig 3), with or without intraretinal hemorrhages, or severe vaso-occlusive pathology (ie, branch or central retinal artery or vein occlusion), which are not seen in the fundus photograph shown in the question stem. In up to 85% of patients, focal segmental glomerulonephritis develops, which if left untreated will incur significant mortality.
Central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma is incorrect; however, always in the differential for posterior uveitis are malignant masquerade syndromes including intraocular lymphoma, retinoblastoma, leukemia, choroidal metastases, and malignant melanoma. If this case presented with primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL) associated with primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL), then the retinal findings would classically include small multifocal subretinal granular infiltrates (Fig 4). Additionally, fluorescein angiography would only show hypofluorescent areas due to blockage from sub-RPE masses or RPE clumping. A leopard-spot pattern with alternating hyper- and hypofluorescence may also be seen. Prognosis is poor for patients with PVRL and CNS involvement with 5-year overall survival of ~60% with treatment.
Tuberculosis (TB) is also incorrect in this classic presentation of APMPPE, however TB should always be in the differential for posterior uveitis (and anterior uveitis). When choroidal involvement occurs, disseminated choroiditis is the most common presentation with multiple (5 to several hundred) discrete yellowish lesions ranging in size (0.5-3.0 mm in diameter) (Figure 5). They may be accompanied by disc edema, hemorrhages in the nerve fiber layer, vitritis, and granulomatous anterior uveitis. Another possible presentation would be a single, large, and elevated choroidal mass (tuberculoma) ranging from 4 mm to 14 mm, with retinal detachment and macular star formation. FA of active choroidal lesions shows early hypo-hyperfluorescence and late leakage (which is not seen in APMPPE); however, cicatricial lesions show early blockage with late staining. Lastly, TB can present with a multifocal choroiditis that has a serpiginoid pattern, also called serpiginous-like choroiditis (Figure 6). Treatment consists of intensive 8-week therapy of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by 18 weeks of isoniazid and rifampin. Substantial mortality is seen with multidrug-resistant TB in HIV-infected patients.

Q2701
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What uveitic condition is characterized by the appearance of blood vessels in the anterior chamber angle without formation of peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS)?
Correct answer: D. Fuchs uveitis syndrome
Rationale
Fuchs uveitis syndrome (sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis [FHI] or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is a chronic, mild, and typically unilateral uveitis associated with secondary open-angle glaucoma. Fine blood vessels are seen in the angle; they bridge the angle structures but do not grow or cause fibrosis like rubeotic vessels.
Posner-Schlossman syndrome, or glaucomatocyclitic crisis, is characterized by recurrent episodes of mild, unilateral iritis with marked elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP) into the 40-60 mm Hg range. With repeated episodes, secondary open-angle glaucoma may develop. As in Fuchs uveitis syndrome, PAS do not develop, but unlike in Fuchs uveitis syndrome, angle vessels are not seen in Posner-Schlossman syndrome.
Synechiae are common in both VKH disease and juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

Q2702
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common ocular manifestation of human T-cell lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1) infection?
Correct answer: C. intermediate uveitis
Rationale
Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a retrovirus of Oncovirinae. It is endemic in Japan, Central and South America, and the Caribbean Islands.
Most cases of HTLV-1 uveitis are intermediate uveitis. Other ocular manifestations are keratoconjunctivitis sicca, retinal infiltrates, and optic neuropathy.

Q2703
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What cell type is primarily responsible for the nature of inflammation seen in ocular sarcoidosis?
Correct answer: A. epithelioid cells
Rationale
Ocular sarcoidosis is characterized by a granulomatous inflammatory reaction due to a specific type of macrophage, the epithelioid cells. While monocytes are very similar to macrophages in function, monocytes are the circulating form of these cells, while macrophages are the tissue-bound form of these cells. Monocytes, therefore, are not responsible for the inflammatory reaction seen in ocular sarcoidosis. Neutrophils and eosinophils do not have a notable role in ocular sarcoidosis.

Q2704
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What uveitis treatment is contraindicated in patients with uveitis associated with multiple sclerosis?
Correct answer: D. tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) inhibitors
Rationale
Up to 30% of multiple sclerosis patients will have evidence of uveitis, and up to 15% of patients with pars planitis will develop multiple sclerosis. TNF-α inhibitors such as etanercept and infliximab are associated with exacerbations of central nervous system demyelination and are therefore contraindicated in patients with demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis. Intravenous and intravitreal corticosteroids and topical cycloplegics are frequently used in the treatment of multiple sclerosis-associated uveitis.

Q2705
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient presents with sudden-onset vision loss in the left eye with the fundus appearance shown. She has truncal and palmar rashes. What is the most appropriate treatment for her condition?
Correct answer: D. penicillin
Rationale
The patient has secondary syphilis, based on presence of palmar and truncal rash in addition to her ocular findings of optic nerve and retinal edema, retinal hemorrhages, and vitritis. In the absence of eye disease, she could be treated with a single dose of intramuscular (IM) benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units. However, patients with syphilitic eye disease should be managed as patients with tertiary syphilis; thus, this patient should receive intravenous penicillin G either continuously or every 4 hours for 10-21 days.

Doxycycline and rifampin are used in combination to treat bartonellosis. Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol are used in combination to treat tuberculosis. Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and folinic acid are used in combination to treat toxoplasmosis.

Q2706
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
In what condition is the use of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α inhibitors in the treatment of uveitis contraindicated?
Correct answer: A. multiple sclerosis
Rationale
TNF-α plays a major role in the pathogenesis of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), ankylosing spondylitis, and other spondyloarthropathies, in addition to inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis. TNF-α inhibitors are biologics approved for the treatment of a number of inflammatory conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, the seronegative spondyloarthropathies, psoriasis including plaque psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, including pediatric Crohn disease. Hidradenitis suppurativa is a painful, long-term skin disease that causes abscesses and skin scarring. TNF-α inhibitors are approved for the treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa.
Multiple adverse effects of TNF-α inhibition have been identified. These include infections, malignancy, injection site reactions, infusion reactions, induction of autoimmunity, demyelinating disease, and heart failure. Thus, use of TNF-α inhibitors is contraindicated in multiple sclerosis, which is a demyelinating disease.

Q2707
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
How does bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) activate the immune system?
Correct answer: B. provocation of innate immune response
Rationale
Bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is an intrinsic component of the cell walls of most gram-negative bacteria. It is one of the most important molecules that trigger the innate immune response. Plasma cell induction, the formation of antibodies, and establishing memory B cells are all part of the more pathogen-specific, targeted, and slower adaptive immune response.

Q2708
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Peripheral necrotizing retinochoroiditis resembling acute retinal necrosis can be seen in patients infected with what pathogen aside from herpesviruses?
Correct answer: C. Treponema pallidum
Rationale
Treponema pallidum

Syphilis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of every individual with uveitis. It is caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum and is associated with numerous ocular manifestations. Posterior segment findings of acquired syphilis include vitritis, chorioretinitis, focal/multifocal retinitis, necrotizing retinochoroiditis, retinal vasculitis, exudative retinal detachment, isolated papillitis, and neuroretinitis. Syphilis may present as a focal retinitis or as a peripheral necrotizing retinochoroiditis that may resemble acute retinal necrosis or progressive outer retinal necrosis.

Q2709
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the recommended treatment for a patient with choroidal candidiasis without vitreous involvement?
Correct answer: D. oral voriconazole
Rationale
When hematogenous dissemination of Candida involves only the choroid, oral triazole antifungals (voriconazole or fluconazole) are effective. When the vitreous is involved, intravitreal antifungals (voriconazole or amphotericin B) should be given, often in conjunction with pars plana vitrectomy.
Oral voriconazole for this particular case is the best option, given that it will have excellent intraocular penetration, and there is no vitreous involvement at this time, so vitrectomy is not required. Periocular or intraocular depot corticosteroid injection should be avoided, because this can make the endophthalmitis worse. Intravitreal injection of an antifungal alone is unlikely to result in adequate treatment of the current chorioretinal lesions, and systemic therapy is warranted.

Q2710
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient with AIDS developed unilateral cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. He was treated with oral valganciclovir and 3 intraocular injections of foscarnet, which halted the retinitis. At that time, his CD4+ T- lymphocyte count was 49 cells/µL. He has since started antiretroviral treatment, with an improvement in CD4+ T- lymphocyte count to 103 cells/µL. He presents with complaints of floaters in the eye with prior CMV and now exhibits a robust vitritis, although the prior area of CMV retinitis looks stable. What is the best initial therapy for this patient's current condition?
Correct answer: A. continuation of oral valganciclovir and starting systemic corticosteroids
Rationale
This patient is likely exhibiting immune recovery uveitis associated with improvement of his CD4+ T- lymphocyte count and ability to mount an inflammatory response to retinal cytomegalovirus (CMV) antigens. Such inflammation can be managed with systemic corticosteroids. The best answer choice listed is to continue oral valganciclovir and start systemic corticosteroids.
Use of periocular steroids should proceed with caution, because there is a chance that there may be a recurrence of the CMV retinitis. Intraocular steroids should be avoided as a first-line therapy for managing immune recovery uveitis. Certainly, if periocular steroids were to be considered, antivirals should be continued. There is no role for pars plana vitrectomy as a first-line therapy for this patient. While there may be a significant amount of vitreous debris associated with inflammation, a trial of systemic corticosteroids may preclude the development of significant debris. Discontinuing antiretroviral therapy is not advisable, as the goal of therapy is to improve the CD4+ T- lymphocyte count and decrease the patient’s overall risk for the development of opportunistic infections.

Q2711
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What establishes the inner blood-ocular barrier?
Correct answer: C. tight junctions between the endothelial cells of the retinal circulation
Rationale
The retinal circulation establishes the inner blood-ocular barrier at the level of the tight junctions between adjacent endothelial cells, while tight junctions between the cells of the retina pigment epithelium provide the outer blood-ocular barrier. There are no lymphatic channels in the inner retina.

Q2712
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
How does the Fas ligand function to create immune privilege in the eye?
Correct answer: C. triggers apoptosis of lymphocytes expressing Fas receptor
Rationale
The Fas ligand is constitutively expressed in the iris and corneal endothelium. It triggers apoptosis of lymphocytes expressing the Fas receptor and is one of the most important mechanisms of effector blockage contributing to immune privilege in the eye.
MHC molecule expression is normally low in the corneal stroma, and increased expression has been linked to corneal graft rejection. Corneal vascularization has also been linked to corneal graft rejection. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) is found in the conjunctiva and is rich in antigen-presenting cells.

Q2713
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 27-year-old patient has bilateral anterior and intermediate uveitis, manifested by keratic precipitates, vitreous cells, and vitreous cellular aggregates near the vitreous base. What test provides the most definitive evidence of sarcoidosis?
Correct answer: B. histopathology of conjunctival nodule, lung specimen, or other involved tissue
Rationale
Each of these diagnostic tests, if positive, support the diagnosis of sarcoidosis. However, the most specific test is histopathology of involved tissue demonstrating noncaseating granulomas. Serum angiotensin-converting-enzyme (ACE) levels are the least specific, as many pulmonary conditions can result in an abnormal test result. Unfortunately, the sensitivity of a "blind" conjunctival biopsy, performed when there is no obvious granuloma, is low; the sensitivity of plain PA and lateral films is higher, and spiral CT is even higher yet. The serum ACE level is moderately sensitive, but the lack of specificity limits the additive information that the ACE would provide when compared to a chest radiograph.

Q2714
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Corneal transplantation has success rates of over 90%, without the need for systemic immunosuppression. What is the reason for this, and what immunoregulatory processes are responsible?
Correct answer: D. immune privilege site, intact limbal physiology, and anterior chamber–associated immune deviation
Rationale
The high success rates of corneal transplantation are due to effective corneal immunoregulation that renders the cornea immune privileged. The 2 major mechanisms that establish this are intact limbal physiology (which prevents blood vessels from crossing over onto the corneal surface) and anterior chamber–associated immune deviation, which attenuates inflammatory reactions in the anterior chamber and on the endothelial surface. The answer choices “effector blockade, attenuated antigen presentation” and “immune privilege site, mucosa-associated lymphatic tissue, and blood–aqueous barrier” are not paired with the proper effector mechanisms. The answer choice “effector blockade, attenuated natural killer cells, and lymphocyte activity”, while paired with the appropriate effectors, does not modulate corneal immune responses, but rather anterior uveal immune responses.

Q2715
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What agent used in the therapy of uveitis may induce antichimeric antibodies?
Correct answer: C. infliximab
Rationale
Infliximab is a mouse/human-chimeric, immunoglobulin G1 kappa (IgG1k) monoclonal antibody directed against tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-a. As many as 75% of patients receiving more than 3 infusions developed antinuclear antibodies, thus causing drug-induced lupus syndrome and the formation of human antichimeric antibodies, which can lead to reduced efficacy of infliximab.
Abatacept is a T-cell costimulation inhibitor given as an intravenous infusion. Interferon alfa-2a/2b (IFN- a2a/b), administered subcutaneously, has been reported to be beneficial in some patients with uveitis. IFN- a2a has antiviral, immunomodulatory, and antiangiogenic effects. Tacrolimus, a product of Streptomyces tsukubaensis, is a calcineurin inhibitor that eliminates T-cell receptor signal transduction and downregulates interleukin-2 gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4+T lymphocytes. Abatacept, IFN- a2a/b, and tacrolimus are not associated with formation of antibodies.

Q2716
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What uveitis therapy has the highest risk of causing secondary glaucoma severe enough to require pressure-lowering surgery?
Correct answer: A. intravitreal fluocinolone 0.59 mg implant
Rationale
Corticosteroids via any route carry the risk of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in predisposed patients. Topical corticosteroids carry the lowest risk. Periocular and intravitreal corticosteroid injections more commonly lead to elevated IOP that requires filtering surgery in 1% to 2% of patients. The intravitreal fluocinolone implant leads to elevated IOP that requires glaucoma therapy in about 75% of patients and glaucoma surgery in about 37% of patients. Antimetabolites such as methotrexate have not been reported to directly lead to elevated IOP.

Q2717
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
The causal relationship between a fungus and ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS) is most supported by what evidence?
Correct answer: C. H. capsulatum DNA has been found in chronic choroidal lesions of a patient with OHS.
Rationale
H. capsulatum DNA has been found in chronic choroidal lesions of a patient with OHS.

The fungus was identified histologically in the choroid of 5 patients with ocular histoplasmosis syndrome. Additionally, more than 90% of patients (not 50%) with the typical fundus appearance react positively to histoplasmin skin testing.
Antifungal therapy has no role in the treatment of choroidal neovascularization associated with ocular histoplasmosis syndrome.
Histoplasma capsulatum is endemic to the Mississippi-Ohio River Valley, not the Rocky Mountain region, and 4.4% of the skin-test responders in this area have the characteristic peripheral lesions of ocular histoplasmosis syndrome.

Q2718
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 24-year-old man from India presents with the finding in the photograph. He has similar findings in the other eye. The macula and optic nerves of both eyes were normal appearing. Laboratory tests show a normal fasting blood sugar, normal serum angiotensin converting enzyme, nonreactive rapid plasma reagin (RPR), negative antinuclear antibody (ANA), negative serum toxoplasmosis antibody, negative Lyme Western-blot, unremarkable chest x-ray, negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), and negative sickle screen. He was born full-term during an uncomplicated pregnancy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. Eales disease
Rationale
Eales disease is a primary occlusive retinopathy with unknown cause. It usually presents in men aged 20-30 years, more commonly in those from India and the Middle East. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is characterized by bilateral idiopathic retinal perivasculitis with peripheral nonperfusion and neovascularization. A sea-fan of peripheral neovascularization may be seen. Vascular sheathing is seen in about 80% of patients, and both arteries and veins may be involved. All patients have confluent peripheral nonperfusion with a sharply demarcated border between perfused and non-perfused peripheral retina. Neovascularization is typically seen at this border and is most commonly found in the temporal quadrant. Vitreous hemorrhage is the most common reason for visual loss, and traction retinal detachments may develop. Treatment is with laser photocoagulation to areas of nonperfused retina. Eales disease has been associated with tuberculin hypersensitivity.
Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV) is an acquired abnormal choroidal vasculopathy (variant of age-related macular degeneration) that clinically presents as hemorrhagic detachments of the pigment epithelium and neurosensory retina. PCV occurs more commonly in persons with darkly pigmented skin, although persons with lighter pigmentation can be affected as well. PCV typically occurs in the peripapillary or macular region although the periphery can be affected as well. The utilization of indocyanine green (ICG) angiography can be helpful in making the diagnosis and visualizing abnormalities within the choroidal vasculature. Management can include observation, photodynamic therapy, anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) intravitreal injections, and rarely surgery.
Coats disease is a sporadic condition that is typically unilateral and has a male predominance (85%). Chromosome 4 has been implicated as the site of the gene involved. Findings include retinal telangiectasia (vascular dilatation) including microaneurysms, fusiform capillary dilatation, venous dilatation, and ectatic arterioles. The vessels are compromised and leak fluid that may cause exudative retinal detachment. Retinal exudates range from minimal to widespread. Consider Coats disease in the differential diagnosis of a child with leukocoria. Treatment of Coats disease includes observation, cryotherapy, photocoagulation, and retinal detachment surgery.
Idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis (IRVAN) is a rare, idiopathic condition characterized by bilateral retinal artery macroaneurysms usually occurring at arterial bifurcations and near the optic nerve. Patients typically present in the third or fourth decade and may also have retinal vasculitis, neuroretinitis, capillary nonperfusion, retinal neovascularization, and macular exudation. Clinical course varies dramatically from benign to severe macular ischemia.

Q2719
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the term for antigenic sites on antibodies?
Correct answer: D. idiotopes
Rationale
Because they are proteins, antibodies themselves can be antigenic. Their antigenic sites are called idiotopes, as distinguished from epitopes, which are the antigenic sites on foreign molecules. An allotope is a site on the constant or nonvarying portion of an antibody molecule that can be recognized by a combining site of other antibodies. An isotope is 1 of 2 or more atoms whose nuclei have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

Q2720
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the best oral induction treatment option for a patient with varicella-zoster virus–associated acute retinal necrosis?
Correct answer: C. valacyclovir 2 g 3 times/day
Rationale
While intravenous acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 10–14 days may be used for induction treatment in acute retinal necrosis, oral valacyclovir 2 g 3 times/day is considered to be an equally efficacious alternative. Oral acyclovir 800 mg 5 times a day, valacyclovir 1 g 3 times a day, or famciclovir 500 mg 3 times a day are the appropriate maintenance doses after induction has been completed. Oral valganciclovir is reserved for cytomegalovirus-associated intraocular infections.

Q2721
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For patients with punctate inner choroidopathy (PIC), what is the most common cause for decreased visual acuity?
Correct answer: D. choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM)
Rationale
Serpiginous choroiditis, multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis (MCP), and PIC all may have visual morbidity secondary to subfoveal and submacular CNVMs. Of these 3 disease entities, PIC has the highest incidence of CNVM at presentation (up to 79%), with subsequent permanent vision loss. However, MCP tends to have a worse visual outcome overall.
An enlarged blind spot can be seen in multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) and related entities (white dot syndromes), and vitritis can be seen but not with PIC. An outer retinitis can be seen with acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR).

Q2722
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the resident macrophage of the retina?
Correct answer: D. microglial cells
Rationale
Tissue-resident macrophages are monocytes that migrated into the tissue during embryologic development and later acquired tissue-specific properties and cellular markers. These resident macrophages are Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lung, and microglia in the brain.
Bipolar cells exist between photoreceptors (rod cells and cone cells) and ganglion cells. They act, directly or indirectly, to transmit signals from the photoreceptors to the ganglion cells.
Amacrine cells are inhibitory neurons, and project their dendritic arbors to the inner plexiform layer (IPL), thereby interacting with retinal ganglion cells and/or bipolar cells.
Horizontal cells are the laterally interconnecting neurons having cell bodies in the inner nuclear layer of the retina of vertebrate eyes. Horizontal cells provide inhibitory feedback to rod and cone photoreceptors.

Q2723
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What laboratory test supports the diagnosis of Lyme disease?
Correct answer: A. serum antibody titers by Western blot
Rationale
Antibody titers by the Western blot technique is one of the laboratory tests used for the diagnosis of Lyme disease. Serum antibody titers by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is another test used. However, due to lack of standardization of positive values, and to cross reactivity with other spirochetes, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends 2 step protocol: ELISA followed by Western blot for testing for active or previous infection. Blood culture and peripheral blood smears are not helpful for the diagnosis of Lyme disease. The rapid plasma reagin test is associated with syphilis infection.

Q2724
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For a patient positive for HLA-A29 and whose fundus and fluorescein angiogram are shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. birdshot chorioretinopathy
Rationale
The characteristic appearance of birdshot chorioretinopathy is multiple creamy, subretinal lesions appearing to radiate from the optic nerve, as demonstrated by this patient. Symptoms may include decreased vision (potentially due to macular edema), photopsias, and other subjective visual disturbance. Carriers of the HLA-A29 genotype have a relative risk of 80 to 100 times compared to the risk of noncarriers. The vitreous infiltrate is typically less pronounced than in the other conditions mentioned. Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome is typically unilateral, and Harada syndrome typically exhibits more prominent vitreous inflammation. The fluorescein angiogram shows cystoid macular edema, which is rarely associated with APMPPE. In addition, APMPPE may be associated with HLA B27 or HLA DR2 but is not associated with HLA-A29.

Q2725
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
In patients with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, the clinical feature of "sunset-glow fundus" is most likely to be found during what stage of the disease?
Correct answer: B. convalescent
Rationale
The photo in the discussion shows Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) disease. Part A shows a color fundus photograph montage of the right eye taken during an acute uveitic phase in a patient with a presenting visual acuity of 20/400 in both eyes. The montage demonstrates vitritis, optic nerve head swelling, diffuse serous detachments with inferior dependency, and dilated and tortuous vasculature. Part B shows montage fundus photographs of the right eye taken 2 years later during the chronic (convalescent) phase. The montage demonstrates diffuse chorioretinal scarring and the classic “sunset glow” fundus due to loss of choroidal pigment. Visual acuity was stable at 20/20 in both eyes.
Diffuse, nonnecrotizing, granulomatous inflammation of the choroid is usually the earliest ocular manifestation of VKH syndrome and occurs during the acute uveitic stage. This can lead to bilateral exudative retinal detachments, also an early sign of this disease.
Sunset-glow fundus occurs when the number of choroidal melanocytes decreases. This occurs during the convalescent stage.
The chronic recurrent stage is characterized by granulomatous choroiditis with damage to the choriocapillaris.

Q2726
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
The treatment of cystoid macular edema associated with active uveitis should begin with what therapy?
Correct answer: A. topical corticosteroid
Rationale
Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a common cause of vision loss in eyes with uveitis. Treatment of CME must first be directed toward control of intraocular inflammation, for which topical steroid remains first-line therapy. If CME persists despite control of inflammation, periocular injection of corticosteroid may be used. Typically, 20-40 mg of triamcinolone is injected into the sub-Tenon space. Anti-VEGF therapies can also reduce inflammatory CME, but the action is short lived and repeat injections are required. Topical NSAIDs can be beneficial in treating pseudophakic CME, but their effectiveness in treating uveitic CME is not established. Oral acetazolamide has been shown to reduce uveitic CME in patients whose uveitis is well controlled.

Q2727
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the reason for diminished intraocular pressure (IOP) in some inflamed eyes?
Correct answer: A. ciliary body hyposecretion
Rationale
In most inflammatory syndromes there is a decrease in intraocular pressure as a result of ciliary body hyposecretion. This makes elevated intraocular pressure in specific uveitis entities such as herpetic uveitis a useful pathognomonic finding that helps in the diagnosis.

Q2728
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Sympathetic ophthalmia can be differentiated from Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome by what feature?
Correct answer: B. history of penetrating ocular trauma
Rationale
Aside from a history of penetrating ocular trauma, sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) and VKH-associated uveitis are essentially identical, as both can manifest meningeal signs (although meningeal signs typically present after ocular inflammation in SO, whereas they precede ocular inflammation in VKH), both are bilateral, both respond well to corticosteroids, and both represent an autoimmune response to tissue pigment. While penetrating ocular trauma was previously thought to be the most common inciting risk factor for developing SO, it is now thought that prior ocular surgery is the most common inciting risk factor, with pars plana vitrectomy having the highest risk at approximately 0.12%.

Q2729
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What antigen does the monoclonal antibody infliximab (Remicade) target?
Correct answer: B. tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α)
Rationale
Infliximab is a humanized murine (chimeric [mouse and human]) monoclonal recombinant antibody that binds TNF-α, a signaling molecule that is central in the inflammatory process. Infliximab is administered intravenously, and the murine portion of the molecule can result in infusion reactions. Adalimumab is another TNF-α inhibitor that is completely humanized and can be administered subcutaneously.
Interleukin-2 is a signaling molecule that regulates T-cell activation, and is inhibited by calcineurin inhibitors such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus.
COX-2 is an enzyme that is involved in prostaglandin synthesis, and is inhibited by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
Choroidal melanoma cells are not targeted with monoclonal antibodies.

Q2730
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What inhibitor of tumor necrosis factor α, useful for treating nonocular inflammation, is less effective for uveitis?
Correct answer: D. etanercept
Rationale
Etanercept, a tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) decoy receptor, has proved effective in controlling joint inflammation in polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) and adult rheumatoid arthritis. It is generally less effective than infliximab and adalimumab for uveitis and is not a preferred biologic for uveitis treatment. There are also some reports of paradoxical inflammation with etanercept. Golimumab is a TNF agonist that is a monoclonal antibody similar to infliximab and adalimumab, but data on its usefulness in uveitis are needed.

Q2731
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What treatment is most appropriate for active bilateral syphilitic panuveitis?
Correct answer: B. intravenous penicillin
Rationale
Intravenous penicillin is the treatment of choice for syphilitic uveitis, and the treatment regimen is the same as for neurosyphilis: 18 to 24 million units per day (MU/d) of aqueous penicillin G (PCN G) for 10 to 14 days. Desensitization and treatment with PCN or ceftriaxone can be considered for PCN-allergic patients.

Q2732
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What systemic disease has the strongest association for uveitis with positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA)?
Correct answer: C. juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Rationale
The presence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) has the strongest association for uveitis in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). The type of JIA-associated uveitis where ANA is positive is the pauciarticular type occurring in young girls. While ANA is part of the criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), lupus is not a frequent cause of uveitis. The presence of ANA can be found in scleroderma, but scleroderma is not a cause of uveitis, although it can cause keratoconjunctivitis sicca related to secondary Sjögren syndrome. Important testing to diagnose tubulointerstitial nephritis-uveitis syndrome includes urine beta-2 microglobulin testing and, if indicated, renal biopsy. Thus, checking ANA in the setting of uveitis is most appropriate in a child with uveitis in whom JIA is suspected.
