A patient presents with bilateral follicular conjunctivitis and mentions that she also has a new rash, as shown below. What organism is responsible?
Correct answer: D. Borrelia burgdorferi
Rationale
Borrelia burgdorferi

Borrelia burgdorferi is the spirochete responsible for Lyme disease. It is transmitted by ticks from animal reservoirs. In stage 1 Lyme disease, about 70% of patients experience a "bull's-eye" macular rash known as erythema chronicum migrans. The most common ocular manifestation of stage 1 disease is a follicular conjunctivitis, occurring in approximately 11% of patients.
Bartonella henselae is responsible for cat-scratch disease, which includes Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome and neuroretinitis.
Treponema pallidum is responsible for syphilis.
Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare can cause infection in patients who are HIV-positive or have AIDS and patients who are severely immunocompromised.

Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is a common manifestation of what white dot syndrome?
Correct answer: C. punctate inner choroidopathy (PIC)
Rationale
PIC occurs more commonly in young, myopic female patients. Patients typically complain of bilateral decreased vision, prominent photopsias, and scotomata. Choroidal neovascularization is a common source of vision loss. Of the white dot syndromes, multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis is associated with CNV development, but less commonly than PIC.
Birdshot chorioretinopathy, APMPPE, and MEWDS are not associated with CNV.

What is the fundus finding in congenital Zika virus infection?
Correct answer: B. retinal pigment mottling and chorioretinal atrophy
Rationale
There have been no reports of uveitis associated with congenital infection. Observed ocular abnormalities include microphthalmia, cataract, glaucoma, iris coloboma, retinal pigment mottling, chorioretinal atrophy, and optic nerve hypoplasia or atrophy. No vaccine exists to prevent Zika at this time. Mosquito-borne transmission of ZIKV has been reported in the United States, and current prevention efforts focus on education and mosquito control.

Q2800

What is the recommended treatment course for most cases of ocular cat-scratch disease?
Correct answer: A. observation
Rationale
Ocular bartonellosis occurs in 5% to 10% of patients with cat-scratch disease (CSD), and includes Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome. The most well-known posterior segment manifestation of B henselae infection is neuroretinitis (although focal retinochoroiditis is the most common uveitic manifestation of CSD).
Definitive treatment guidelines have not emerged for CSD, because it is a self-limiting illness in most cases, with an overall excellent systemic and visual prognosis. The efficacy of antibiotics has not been conclusively demonstrated.
The efficacy of oral corticosteroids on the course of systemic and ocular disease is unknown.

Q2801
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient is being treated for first-time presentation of undifferentiated granulomatous iridocyclitis. The patient responds very well to hourly topical corticosteroid, but in the past 3 months, the patient's intraocular inflammation has recurred every time the ophthalmologist has tried to taper the steroid below 4 times/day. The patient is beginning to develop a posterior subcapsular cataract, and her intraocular pressure is now 23 mm Hg on 1 glaucoma drop. What would be the most appropriate next step?
Correct answer: B. Increase topical corticosteroids and initiate therapy with an antimetabolite (eg, methotrexate).
Rationale
Although her increasing intraocular pressure is a concern, there are other options available to help control her intraocular inflammation and pressure, while avoiding surgery. On the other hand, simply increasing her topical corticosteroid and starting oral acetazolamide will only serve to temporize the same issue: namely, the patient needs a steroid-sparing agent to keep her intraocular inflammation under control and spare her the side effects of steroids. Tapering the steroid and providing reassurance is incorrect, given that the patient's inflammation has flared up when the ophthalmologist has tried to taper the dosing below 4 times per day. The correct option here would be to increase the topical corticosteroids to get her inflammation back under control, start some form of immunomodulatory therapy (typically an antimetabolite to start with) to maintain control of her inflammation while tapering the steroid, and manage her intraocular pressure during this time.

Q2802

By what mode is the chikungunya virus typically transmitted to humans?

Rationale
Chikungunya fever, a potentially fatal illness, is caused by single-stranded RNA virus of the genus Alphavirus, in the family Togaviridae. It is transmitted via infected mosquitoes including Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus.
Toxoplasma gondii can be transmitted via ingestion of contaminated water, fruit, or vegetables with oocysts.
HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B virus, and hepatitis C virus are among the diseases transmitted by contact with blood or bodily fluids.
Common pathogens transmitted via drinking water are norovirus, Giardia, Legionella, Salmonella, and Escherichia coli.

What immunosuppressive agent commonly used as a corticosteroid-sparing agent for ocular inflammatory disease is most likely to have gingival hyperplasia as an unwanted side effect?
Correct answer: D. cyclosporine
Rationale
Gingival hyperplasia is one of the well-known side effects specific to cyclosporine therapy. Cyclophosphamide is typically associated with leukopenia, hemorrhagic cystitis, sterility, and reversible alopecia. Azathioprine and methotrexate are both antimetabolites typically associated with gastrointestinal discomfort and hepatotoxicity.

Q2804

A 56-year-old woman with bilateral recurrent idiopathic anterior and intermediate uveitis has been stable on 10 mg/day of systemic prednisone and 15 mg/week of methotrexate for 3 months. Dual energy x-ray absorptiometry [DXA]) shows normal age-matched levels. What additional treatment should be recommended?
Correct answer: B. Add calcium and vitamin D supplementation.
Rationale
This is a patient with controlled uveitis. It is advisable to spare steroids in the treatment of uveitis as much as possible; however, low doses of steroids, such as 7.5 mg/day, are permissible as long as there are no steroid-related complications. Stopping the steroids suddenly or switching to azathioprine may exacerbate uveitis.
American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Task Force osteoporosis guidelines suggest that patients taking glucocorticoids (any dose with an anticipated duration of ≥3 months) maintain a total calcium intake of 1200 mg/day and vitamin D intake of 800 international units/day through diet and/or supplements.
Patients with the highest risk for fracture, determined by a combination of bone mineral density (BMD) and clinical risk factors, are the ones most likely to benefit from drug therapy with bisphosphonates like zoledronic acid.

An immunosuppressed patient presents with features consistent with unilateral endophthalmitis. A diagnostic and therapeutic pars plana vitrectomy is performed, and inspection of the vitreous reveals septate, dichotomously branching hyphae on silver stain. What is the most likely organism?
Correct answer: A. Aspergillus fumigatus
Rationale
Aspergillus fumigatus

Septate, dichotomously branching hyphae are seen in Aspergillus. Cryptococcus does not appear as hyphae, but as round capsules with a halo (on India ink), while periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain the organism and leave the capsule unstained. Candida albicans are budding yeast with a pseudohyphate appearance. Bartonella henselae is a bacterium associated with cat scratch disease-associated neuroretinitis. It is a gram-negative bacterium best identified with the Warthin-Starry stain.

Q2806
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
By what mechanism is mycophenolate mofetil thought to ameliorate autoimmune uveitis?
Correct answer: D. inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and DNA synthesis
Rationale
Mycophenolate mofetil inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase, which prevents the synthesis of the purine nucleotide guanosine. This prevents B and T lymphocyte synthesis, and leads to aberrant base pairing, ring cleavage, and depurination, which leads to cell death. Inhibition of bacterial ribosomes characterizes the mechanism of action of some antibiotics (for example streptomycin, erythromycin, and chloramphenicol).
Therapies that reliably induce immunologic tolerance in autoinflammatory conditions are being developed, but they have yet to show efficacy in uveitis.

Q2807

What class of infectious organisms has been associated with glaucomatocyclitic crisis (also known as Posner-Schlossman syndrome)?
Correct answer: C. viruses such as cytomegalovirus (CMV)
Rationale
Glaucomatocyclitic crisis has been associated with CMV infection, and the virus has been isolated from the eyes of patients with this disease. Topical corticosteroids and aqueous suppressants are used to treat the episodes of acute anterior uveitis and intraocular pressure elevation in these patients. Presenting intraocular pressure can be very high (> 40 mm Hg) during these episodes. The inflammation responds readily to topical corticosteroids.

Q2808
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 65-year-old man is found to have unilateral decline in vision as well as occlusive arteritis, vitritis, and a multifocal yellow-white peripheral retinitis. What is the best therapy?
Correct answer: C. systemic acyclovir
Rationale
Patients with acute retinal necrosis usually present with acute unilateral loss of vision, photophobia, floaters, and pain. Panuveitis is observed, beginning with significant anterior segment inflammation with keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae, and elevated intraocular pressure, together with heavy vitreous cellular infiltration. Within 2 weeks, the classic triad of occlusive retinal arteriolitis, vitritis, and a multifocal yellow-white peripheral retinitis has evolved. Widespread necrosis of the midperipheral retina, multiple posterior retinal breaks, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy predispose to combined tractional–rhegmatogenous retinal detachments in 75% of patients. Timely diagnosis and prompt antiviral therapy are essential given the rapidity of disease progression, the frequency of retinal detachment, and the guarded visual prognosis.
Intravenous acyclovir, 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 10–14 days, is effective against herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus. After 24–48 hours of antiviral therapy, systemic corticosteroids (prednisone, 1 mg/kg/day) are introduced to treat active inflammation and subsequently tapered over several weeks. Aspirin and other anticoagulants have been used to treat an associated hypercoagulable state and prevent vascular occlusions, but the results have been inconclusive. More recently, oral valacyclovir at doses of up to 2 g, 3 times daily, has been used successfully as an alternative to intravenous acyclovir as induction therapy. Additionally, intravitreal ganciclovir (0.2–2.0 mg/0.1 mL) and foscarnet (1.2–2.4 mg/0.1 mL) have been used to achieve a rapid induction in combination with both intravenous and oral antivirals as first-line therapy or in patients who fail to respond to systemic acyclovir.

Q2809
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Under what condition would cataract surgery be appropriate in a patient with active uveitis?
Correct answer: A. phacolytic uveitis
Rationale
Phacolytic uveitis refers to high-molecular weight lens proteins leaking out of the capsule into the anterior chamber, thereby inciting reactive inflammation. This inflammation can be associated with elevated intraocular pressure, and, notably, there is a lack of keratic precipitates. Cataract extraction is the definitive treatment for this condition. If a cataract is associated with the other conditions listed, the cause may be either active or poorly controlled inflammation or exposure to topical, periocular, intraocular, and, less often, systemic corticosteroids. In the setting of these types of noninfectious uveitides, cataract surgery is typically performed when the inflammation has been quiet for at least 3 months.

Q2810

What is the prevailing theory of the molecular pathogenesis of sympathetic ophthalmia (SO)?
Correct answer: B. autoimmune response to a previously sequestered antigen
Rationale
The etiology of SO is unknown. Although an infectious agent has been speculated through molecular mimicry of an endogenous ocular antigen, no organism has been consistently isolated. Animal studies, however, support the notion that SO may result from altered T-lymphocyte responses to previously sequestered ocular self-antigens, such as retinal S-antigen, interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein, melanin-associated antigens, and antigens derived from the retina pigment epithelium (RPE) or choroid following ocular injury.

Q2811
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common infectious cause of a unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis with lymphadenopathy?
Correct answer: D. Bartonella henselae
Rationale
Bartonella henselae

Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome, or granulomatous conjunctivitis and ipsilateral lymphadenopathy, is typically associated with Bartonella infection, or cat scratch disease. Francisella tularensis, the organism responsible for tularemia, is also a possible etiology, as are syphilis, tuberculosis, and sporotrichosis, but these are all uncommon. Adult chlamydial inclusion conjunctivitis may be considered but the conjunctival reaction is follicular rather than granulomatous. Streptococcus does not cause a granulomatous conjunctivitis.

Q2812
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 48-year-old patient has nyctalopia and decreased vision. Given the color photo and angiographic image shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. birdshot retinochoroidopathy
Rationale
Patients with birdshot retinochoroidopathy present with blurred vision, floaters, and nyctalopia. Funduscopy reveals characteristic multifocal, hypopigmented, ovoid, cream-colored lesions at the level of the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in postequatorial, mostly nasal fundus in a radial pattern, as shown in the images (Fig. 1). Cystoid macular edema (CME), as shown in the fundus fluorescein angiogram (FA) below, is a common reason for decreased vision in these patients and a sign of disease activity.
Punctate inner choroiditis (PIC) commonly presents in otherwise healthy myopic white women at a younger median age (29-45 years). Lesions of PIC rarely extend to the midperiphery, and CME is uncommon. Choroidal neovascularization is a common vision-threatening complication.
Intraocular lymphoma mainly affects older patients, in the fifth to seventh decade of life. The lesions are creamy yellow subretinal infiltrates with overlying RPE detachments. CME is uncommon.
Lesions in MEWDS are distributed perifoveally and are discrete, white-orange spots (as shown in Fig. 2). Fluorescein angiography shows a characteristic punctate hyperfluorescence in a wreathlike configuration. The prognosis is favorable, with visual recovery within 2 to 10 weeks.

Q2813
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What test is an indicator of active infection in syphilis disease?
Correct answer: D. rapid plasma reagin (RPR)
Rationale
The serum rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test can be an indicator of active syphilitic infection but does not confirm that a patient has syphilis; for that, a treponemal test, such as the fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) assay and the microhemagglutination assay for T pallidum antibodies (MHA‑TP) is needed. FTA-ABS and MHA-TP are treponemal antigen tests that do not correlate with disease activity, and the results of those tests may be positive for a lifetime. Eye fluid culture is not used for the diagnosis of any stage of syphilis.

Q2814
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What method of intraocular pressure control should be avoided in a patient with chronic anterior uveitis?
Correct answer: C. laser trabeculoplasty
Rationale
Laser trabeculoplasty is not effective in managing intraocular patients with chronic anterior uveitis, because the laser can potentiate inflammation. Additionally, appropriate laser placement to the trabecular meshwork may not be possible if peripheral anterior synechiae are present. First-line therapy for managing intraocular pressure includes aqueous suppression with topical or oral medication. For intraocular pressure recalcitrant to medical therapy, surgery should be considered. Trabeculectomy can be considered, especially if inflammation is well controlled. Mitomycin C can help in the prevention of scarring. Alternatively, a tube shunt can be placed.

Q2815
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 62-year-old patient presents with uveitis that has not responded to prolonged steroid therapy. He has vitreous haze without a clear view of the fundus. What is the next best step to obtain a diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. vitreous biopsy
Rationale
The presence of vitreous cells in cases of uveitis not responding to therapy necessitates a vitreous biopsy. An MRI of the brain is indicated to determine central nervous system (CNS) involvement, even in suspected primary intraocular lymphoma, regardless of the presence or absence of neurologic symptoms, but a vitreous specimen should be obtained as a primary step. HLA testing would not be indicated as an initial step in workup, and a fluorescein angiogram is unlikely to provide useful information in confirming a diagnosis of primary CNS lymphoma.

Q2816
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Chronic uveitis after cataract surgery, when it is attributed to the intraocular lens (IOL), is most commonly caused by what problem?
Correct answer: D. malposition of the intraocular lens
Rationale
Intraocular inflammation is typically attributed to the mechanical chafing effect of a malpositioned intraocular lens, not to the lens material itself. Chronic postoperative endophthalmitis, such as that associated with Propionibacterium acnes sequestered in the capsular bag, typically presents with chronic inflammation that persists beyond the initial postoperative period and should be considered on the differential diagnosis. Incorrect IOL power would not cause uveitis.

Q2817
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common ocular complication of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection?
Correct answer: C. HIV retinopathy
Rationale
The ocular manifestations in systemic HIV infection include HIV-related microangiopathy of the retina; opportunistic viral, bacterial, and fungal infections; Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas of the retina, adnexa, and orbit; and squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva. HIV retinopathy is the most common ocular finding in patients with AIDS; it is seen in up to 70% of cases.

Q2818
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 29-year-old woman presents for evaluation of bilateral central vision loss and photopsias. She reports onset of fever, chills, headache, and malaise approximately 1 week ago. The ophthalmologist notes the fundus findings shown in the image, as well as corresponding early hypofluorescence and late-phase staining. What life-threatening complication is associated with the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
Correct answer: D. cerebral vasculitis
Rationale
Lesions of acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) are associated with loss of vision with central or paracentral scotomas and photopsias. Approximately half of affected patients have a preceding viral prodrome, and men and women are affected equally. Symptoms are typically bilateral, with fellow eye involvement occurring within a period of days to weeks. Typical fundus findings include large (1-2 disc diameters), yellow-white, placoid lesions distributed throughout the posterior pole to the equator. Fundus angiography typically demonstrates early hypofluorescence corresponding to the lesions but often exceeding the areas visible funduscopically. In late phases, these lesions demonstrate late hypofluorescent staining. These lesions typically involute over a period of several weeks, leaving behind significant retinal pigment epithelial alteration.
Most patients recover visual function of 20/40 or better, although there are often residual visual deficits. APMPPE is associated with HLA-B7 and HLA-DR2 and is thought to be an immune-driven vasculitis. The most serious complication associated with APMPPE is the development of cerebral vasculitis.

Q2819
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 52-year-old man presents with bilateral panuveitis and retinal vasculitis. He also has complaints of arthralgia, diplopia, diarrhea, and poor performance at work. What test may help with the diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. duodenal biopsy
Rationale
Whipple disease is a rare multisystem disease caused by the Tropheryma whipplei bacterium. It is most common in middle-aged white men. Migratory arthritis occurs in 80% of cases, and diarrhea, steatorrhea, and malabsorption occur in 75%. Central nervous system involvement occurs in 10% of cases and results in seizures, dementia, and coma. Neuro-ophthalmic signs can include cranial nerve palsies, nystagmus, and ophthalmoplegia. Intraocular involvement occurs in less than 5% of cases. Patients can present with bilateral panuveitis, retinal vasculitis, and multifocal chorioretinitis. The gold standard for diagnosis of Whipple disease is a duodenal biopsy that demonstrates a periodic acid–Schiff–positive bacillus in macrophages within intestinal villi.

Q2820
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Band keratopathy is a common complication in what form of uveitis?
Correct answer: B. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)-associated anterior uveitis
Rationale
Band keratopathy is a complication of chronic intraocular inflammation, typically more common when the predominant site of inflammation is the anterior segment. Of the choices provided, only JIA-associated anterior uveitis is a chronic uveitis. HLA-B27-associated uveitis and herpetic iridocyclitis are both acute, episodic forms of uveitis and typically do not result in band keratopathy (Note: inadequately treated forms of B27 acute anterior uveitis can take on a more "chronic" nature that can eventually produce band keratopathy, but this is not common). Toxoplasma-associated uveitis is predominantly a posterior uveitis that is also episodic in nature and does not typically result in band keratopathy. Aggressive inflammation associated with toxoplasmosis can produce anterior segment inflammation, as well, but the episodic nature of this type of inflammation precludes the chronic inflammation necessary to produce band keratopathy.

Q2821
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What immunosuppressive drug used to treat noninfectious ocular inflammation is most clearly associated with an increased risk of malignancy?
Correct answer: B. cyclophosphamide
Rationale
Alkylating agents include cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil. The most worrisome adverse effect of these agents is an increased risk of malignancy. There drugs should be used with great caution.
Azathioprine and methotrexate are antimetabolites, and cyclosporine is a T-cell inhibitor. The Systemic Immunosuppressive Therapy for Eye Diseases (SITE) cohort study of 7957 patients with noninfectious uveitis showed that patients who took azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, or systemic corticosteroids had overall cancer mortality rates similar to those who never took those medications. There was a non-statistically significant increase in cancer-related mortality rates in patients treated with cyclophosphamide.

Q2822
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
In what stage of syphilis infection can a syphilitic gumma be seen?
Correct answer: C. tertiary
Rationale
Gummatous syphilis is very uncommon in the present era. Gummas are heaped up granulomatous lesions with a round, irregular, or serpiginous shape. They can occur anywhere, including skin, bones, or internal organs. Gummatous syphilis remains the most uncommon type of tertiary syphilis. Other subcategories of tertiary syphilis include cardiovascular syphilis and neurosyphilis, with ocular syphilis being considered a variant of the latter.

Q2823
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What tissue is more effectively evaluated with indocyanine green angiography than with fluorescein angiography?
Correct answer: C. choroid
Rationale
Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) is used to evaluate the choroid, including choroidal perfusion and lesions within the choroid.
Imaging of the inner retina is best performed with optical coherence tomography. The pars plana is best imaged with wide-field fundus photography and fluorescein angiography. The ciliary body can be evaluated at least in part with gonioscopy, but anterior segment ultrasound biomicroscopy is excellent at imaging this structure.

Q2824
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 68-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with severe lung disease. He reports sudden pain and vision loss in the right eye and is noted to have a macular infiltrate with a subretinal hypopyon and involvement of retinal and choroidal vessels. Minimal vitritis is present and the anterior segment is relatively quiet. What fungal pathogen is most likely causative?
Correct answer: D. Aspergillus
Rationale
Aspergillus

Endogenous Aspergillus endophthalmitis is typically seen in patients with severe chronic pulmonary disease, immunocompromise, endocarditis, or intravenous (IV) drug abuse. Disseminated infection most commonly involves the lung, with the eye as the second most common site of infection.
Unlike Candida endophthalmitis, in which the vitreous is the main focus of infection, the main foci of Aspergillus infections are the subretinal space and retinal and choroidal vessels. Because Aspergillus often involves the macula, visual outcomes are poor.
Ocular coccidioidomycosis is rare and typically manifests with blepharitis, phlyctenular and granulomatous conjunctivitis, or more uncommonly, with granulomatous anterior uveitis, iris granulomas, or multifocal chorioretinitis.
Ocular cryptococcus is often seen in patients with HIV and is frequently associated with meningitis. Papilledema, cranial nerve palsies, and multifocal chorioretinitis are seen.

Q2825
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What intervention is most likely to limit the inflammatory sequelae of ocular cysticercosis?
Correct answer: B. removal via vitrectomy
Rationale
Death of the larvae results in significant intraocular inflammation. As such, removal of the intraocular cyst via vitrectomy, without killing the contained larvae, results in the least amount of intraocular inflammation.

Q2826
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common form of intraocular involvement in patients with sarcoid panuveitis?
Correct answer: C. chronic anterior uveitis
Rationale
Although all of these features can be seen in ocular sarcoidosis, chronic anterior uveitis is the most frequently encountered form (up to 80% in some series).
Posterior segment manifestations occur in up to 20% of patients with ocular sarcoidosis. Vitreous involvement is common and often presents as clumps of snowballs with or without diffuse cellular infiltration. Occlusive retinal vascular disease, especially branch retinal vein occlusion and, less commonly, central retinal vein occlusion, together with peripheral retinal capillary nonperfusion, may lead to retinal neovascularization and vitreous hemorrhage. Sarcoid may also be associated with an inflammatory optic neuropathy, with or without concurrent intraocular inflammation.

Q2827
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What finding in vitreous samples can help to support the diagnosis of intraocular lymphoma?
Correct answer: B. high ratio of IL-10 to IL-6
Rationale
Cytokine analysis of vitreous samples can be helpful in supporting the diagnosis of intraocular lymphoma. Interleukin-10 (IL-10) levels are elevated in the vitreous of patients with lymphoma. In contrast, high levels of IL-6 are found in the vitreous of patients with inflammatory uveitis. Thus, the ratio of IL-10 to IL-6 is often elevated in intraocular lymphoma and supports the diagnosis. Gene rearrangement studies can provide evidence of monoclonality. Flow cytometry may reveal kappa (κ) or gamma (γ) chain restriction or large B-cell populations, both of which support the diagnosis of B-cell lymphoma. A specific mutation (proline for leucine substitution mutation at position 265) of the myeloid differentiation primary response 88 protein (MYD88) is also supportive.
If diagnosis by vitreous aspiration or subretinal aspiration cannot be established, internal or external chorioretinal biopsy techniques may be useful in the diagnosis of PCNSL.
Cytologic specimens obtained from the vitreous or subretinal space often show pleomorphic cells with scanty cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei with multiple irregular nucleoli, and an elevated nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio. Monoclonality of cells is likely to be present in PCNSL. This can be established through immunophenotyping by immunohistochemistry or flow cytometry to demonstrate the clonality of B lymphocytes by the presence of abnormal immunoglobulin κ or γ light chain predominance, specific B-lymphocyte markers (CD19, CD20, and CD22), and/or gene or oncogene translocations or gene rearrangements. Abnormal lymphocytes may be isolated manually or by laser capture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR)–based assays performed to improve the diagnostic yield of paucicellular samples. See also BCSC Section 4, Ophthalmic Pathology and Intraocular Tumors, for discussion of intraocular lymphoma.

Q2828
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is an expected side effect associated with a tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) inhibitor?
Correct answer: C. increased risk of infection
Rationale
Because TNF-α inhibitors interfere with the TNF signaling pathway involved in mediating inflammation (which can be an important response in fighting infection), the use of such medications can increase the patient's susceptibility to infection. Thus, tuberculosis is typically evaluated prior to starting an anti-TNF medication. Additionally, it is important to determine whether patients at risk for certain fungal infections live in an area where those infections are endemic.

Q2829
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What ocular finding would be expected in a patient infected with chikungunya virus?
Correct answer: A. uveitis
Rationale
The ocular features of chikungunya virus infection include anterior uveitis and retinitis. The anterior uveitis may be characterized by pigmented keratic precipitates, iris pigment release, and, like other types of viral anterior uveitides, elevated intraocular pressure. Varying amounts of vitritis can be seen, and the posterior segment findings involve a retinitis characterized by focal, multifocal, or confluent retinitis, occasionally with retinal hemorrhages.

Q2830
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 72-year-old man reports several episodes of vision loss in his right eye over the past few months. He has no ocular history other than uncomplicated cataract surgery in both eyes 3 years ago. The patient has covered either eye and confirms that the vision loss is isolated to his right eye. He describes the vision loss as a "white out" that comes on over several minutes, leaves him severely visually disabled for several hours, and then gradually clears back to his normal baseline vision over 1 to 2 hours. He has had eye examinations following each of these episodes in the past. They showed mild phacodonesis in the right eye but were otherwise unremarkable. Prior workup to rule out giant cell arteritis was negative. The patient is frustrated that despite multiple examinations, an etiology has not been found. What would be the most helpful thing to do on his visit today to help yield a diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. gonioscopy
Rationale
Whenever a patient complains of vision loss in 1 eye only, it is imperative to know whether the visual loss involves the right eye or the right field of vision. Unless a patient has covered each eye alternately, they cannot know this. In this question, the patient was reliable and had confirmed the vision loss was only in 1 eye. The second issue is the nature of the vision loss. Amaurosis fugax is characterized by temporary loss of all sight in the eye (a "blackout"). However, this patient describes a "white out," which is more characteristic of a transient obscuring of the ocular media, especially considering the long duration of the vision loss and the slow recovery over 1-2 hours.
In any patient with symptoms suggestive of transient obscuring of the ocular media, who is also pseudophakic, uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome should be considered. In UGH syndrome, chafing of the iris by the optic/bag complex or the haptics causes transient intraocular bleeds. Gonioscopy is the key to the diagnosis of UGH, especially after the vision has cleared. A small layer of hemorrhage in the inferior angle provides evidence of the transient bleed. Although originally described as a complication of iris chafing by closed-loop anterior chamber intraocular lenses (IOLs), UGH syndrome is now more commonly seen with PCIOLs.
Automated visual field testing would be beneficial if a homonymous defect were suspected, as opposed to loss of vision restricted to 1 eye. Likewise, referral to cardiology for a Holter monitor would be beneficial if symptoms consistent with vertebro-basilar insufficiency were suspected; however, loss of vision restricted to 1 eye makes this less likely.

Q2831
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the cause of hypotony in chronic anterior uveitis?
Correct answer: B. decreased aqueous production from the ciliary body
Rationale
Dysfunction of the ciliary body may be a sequela of chronic inflammation; this may be due to ciliary body detachment induced by cyclitic membranes, reversible dysfunction due to inflammation, or permanent dysfunction in the setting of ciliary body atrophy.
Anterior synechiae and posterior synechiae may lead to elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), but in some patients may be part of a delicate balance of decreased aqueous production and outflow; these patients may develop hypotony following intraocular surgery if aqueous outflow is improved.
Corticosteroids can increase IOP by reversing ciliary body dysfunction induced by inflammation or choroidal effusion, or by corticosteroid-induced glaucoma.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2832
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 55-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of right eye pain and photophobia. On examination, there is mild injection of the bulbar conjunctiva, and 2+ cell and flare with no keratic precipitates. Her left eye is white and quiet. The ophthalmologist diagnoses nongranulomatous anterior uveitis. On review of systems, she notes that her knees have been very painful recently, and the ophthalmologist orders a number of tests. All test results are negative except for a positive anti-CCP (cyclic citrullinated protein antibodies) test result. What systemic disease is most likely?
Correct answer: C. rheumatoid arthritis
Rationale
This patient has a positive CCP test result. In addition to the rheumatoid factor (RF) test, the CCP test is helpful in diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis. The sensitivity and specificity is increased when both RF and CCP show positive results, but in the setting of painful joints, rheumatoid arthritis is the most likely diagnosis.
The spectrum of ocular findings in Lyme disease varies with stage of disease. Anterior, intermediate, or posterior uveitis, or panuveitis, may occur in Stage 2 Lyme disease. Intermediate uveitis is the most common presentation.
Tubulointerstitial nephritis occurs most commonly in adolescent girls, and a bilateral nongranulomatous anterior uveitis is the most common presentation. Workup reveals abnormal serum creatinine levels and abnormal urinalysis results, with elevated beta-2 microglobulin levels, proteinuria, and urinary white cell casts. Anterior uveitis is the most common ocular presentation of sarcoidosis.
The work up of sarcoidosis includes chest Xray or chest computed tomography (CT) scan, lysozyme level, and serum angiotensin converting enzyme level.

Q2833
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Following resolution of the white dots, what finding suggests the diagnosis of multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS)?
Correct answer: C. granular pigment changes in the fovea
Rationale
Subtle granular pigment changes in the fovea are present after the acute stage of MEWDS and they are considered pathognomonic for the disease. The finding can be very useful in diagnosing patients who present with symptoms after the white dots have faded. MEWDS patients do not typically develop peripheral punched-out lesions or peripapillary scarring, which can be present in ocular histoplasmosis syndrome and multifocal choroiditis. Perivascular pigment alterations can be present in retinal vasculitis, but not in MEWDS.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2834
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What disorder is most likely to cause a low-grade, unilateral, chronic, anterior uveitis and be associated with iris atrophy and transillumination defects?
Correct answer: D. viral anterior uveitis
Rationale
Hallmark features of viral iridocyclitis include low-grade, chronic cells; diffuse, tiny keratic precipitates (KP) that do not remain within the Arlt triangle; iris atrophy; iris transillumination; and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) during active flare-ups. A feature more specific to herpetic iridocyclitis is the presence of larger KP with overlying stromal edema secondary to the associated underlying endothelial dysfunction (ie, disciform keratitis). Although herpetic disease comes to mind in considering these examination findings, any viral iridocyclitis can present with these findings (except disciform keratitis, which is more specific to herpetic disease), although not as pronounced as when they occur with herpetic disease.
HLA-B27–associated acute anterior uveitis (AAU) can present with large keratic precipitates, a dense and fibrinous anterior chamber reaction with associated formation of posterior synechiae, and a hypopyon, but iris atrophy and transillumination are not typical of HLA-B27–associated disease.
VKH typically presents with bilateral exudative retinal detachments. Upon resolution of these detachments, future flare-ups do tend to present as low-grade anterior chamber reactions, but there is no associated iris atrophy or transillumination.
Sarcoidosis can present anywhere in the eye and can produce nongranulomatous and granulomatous inflammation (although the disease itself is granulomatous in nature); however, it does not result in iris atrophy or transillumination.

Q2835
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common ocular manifestation of syphilis?
Correct answer: D. uveitis
Rationale
Syphilis is the "great imitator," but uveitis is the most common ocular manifestation or component of presentation. All of the other inflammatory features (localized choroiditis, cystoid macular edema, and neuroretinitis) may be present at a lesser frequency.

Q2836
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common cause of vision loss in pars planitis?
Correct answer: C. cystoid macular edema
Rationale
Pars planitis refers to intermediate uveitis that is idiopathic. Cystoid macular edema is the number one cause of vision loss in pars planitis and can be chronic and refractory in up to 10% of patients. Other causes of vision loss in pars planitis include cataract, epiretinal membrane, and vitreous opacification. Vitreous hemorrhage can occur due to neovascularization in the peripheral retina but is not a common cause of vision loss. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments can occur but are less common than serous or tractional detachments. Pars plana exudates, or snowbanks, can be seen in pars planitis and may indicate a more severe course, but they are not a major cause of vision loss.

Q2837
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What finding would be an indication for systemic immunomodulatory therapy in a child with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)-associated iritis?
Correct answer: B. chronic anterior chamber cells on maximally tolerated local corticosteroid therapy
Rationale
The initial treatment of patients with JIA-associated uveitis includes topical corticosteroids. More severe cases require the use of systemic or periocular corticosteroids. However, long-term use of systemic corticosteroids can lead to complications such as growth retardation. Due to high ocular morbidity, these children should be treated with weekly, low-dose methotrexate. Methotrexate is effective, well tolerated and spares the complications associated with chronic ocular inflammation and systemic complications of corticosteroids. Recent studies also have shown the efficacy of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors in children with uveitis.
Presence of ANA is a risk factor for chronic iridocyclitis in patients with JIA, but is not an indication for systemic treatment in the absence of uveitis.
Posterior synechiae and band keratopathy are some of the ocular complications of JIA-associated uveitis, but not an indication for systemic treatment unless there is active uveitis.

Q2838
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For about how long does the fluocinolone acetonide implant release therapeutic levels of corticosteroids to the vitreous cavity?
Correct answer: D. 30 months
Rationale
Multicenter, controlled clinical studies have shown that the 0.59-mg fluocinolone implant is effective for a median of 30 months. The sustained-release implant was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2005 for the treatment of chronic noninfectious uveitis affecting the posterior segment. The implant is inserted through a small pars plana incision and sutured to the sclera.

Q2839
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A woman with anterior and intermediate sarcoid uveitis exhibits less than ½+ anterior chamber cells, minimal vitreous haze, and no macular edema on mycophenolate and infliximab treatment. Before treatment, she exhibited 3+ anterior chamber cells, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, extensive posterior synechiae without iris bombé, and 2+ vitreous haze in both eyes. She now needs cataract surgery to drive. What is the best approach to cataract surgery?
Correct answer: A. Wait until her level of inflammation is stable on this regimen for at least 3 months and then perform cataract surgery.
Rationale
Ensuring that the current regimen is effective in controlling inflammation for at least 3 months and allowing the ocular tissues to recover from recent inflammation are both highly desirable. In some cases, it might not be necessary to wait 3 months; examples include a very mild uveitis that was easily controlled and is without sequelae as well as Fuchs heterochromic uveitis, which has a good surgical prognosis. The fluocinolone implant is unnecessary in this case because she is already being treated systemically, her disease is well controlled, and there is no macular edema. Reduction of anterior chamber cells to zero for 6 months is unnecessary.

Q2840
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the classic histologic description of phacoantigenic uveitis?
Correct answer: C. zonal granulomatous reaction
Rationale
The typical histopathological appearance of phacoantigenic uveitis is a zonal granuloma centered around the site of the lens injury; neutrophils are present with surrounding lymphocytes, plasma cells, epithelioid cells, and occasional giant cells.
Macrophages with engorged lens proteins are thought to be the mechanism of trabecular meshwork obstruction in phacolytic glaucoma.
A purely polymorphonuclear leukocyte reaction is not typical, and an eosinophilic reaction is also not typical; for this reason, the old term phacoanaphylactic uveitis is not appropriate for this condition, because anaphylaxis involves immunoglobulin E (IgE), mast cells, and basophils, none of which are present in phacoantigenic uveitis.

Q2841
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common noninfectious systemic disease associated with scleritis?
Correct answer: A. rheumatoid arthritis
Rationale
About 40% of scleritis cases are associated with systemic disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and systemic lupus erythematosus are also associated with scleritis, but much less frequently. Multiple sclerosis is associated with intermediate uveitis and pars planitis, not scleritis.

Q2842
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What white blood cell can become an antigen-presenting cell?
Correct answer: D. monocyte
Rationale
Basophils, eosinophils, and neutrophils do not have the ability to act as antigen-presenting cells. Only monocytes can be primed and induced to become antigen-presenting cells.

Q2843

What osteoporosis therapy is most strongly implicated as a cause of ocular inflammatory disease?
Correct answer: C. alendronate
Rationale
Bisphosphonates (such as alendronate, etidronate, risedronate, and zoledronic acid) have been associated with the development of uveitis. Other medications that have been associated with uveitis include oral contraceptives, rifabutin, sulfonamides, diethylcarbamazine, etanercept, topical metipranolol, topical prostaglandin analogues (PGAs), intravitreal cidofovir, and intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections.

Q2844
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 50-year-old man with a history of open-globe repair as a child presents with blurred vision and photophobia. Examination reveals bilateral panuveitis and subtle hypopigmented deep subretinal lesions. What is the most appropriate first step in treatment for the most likely cause of these findings?
Correct answer: A. oral corticosteroid
Rationale
Sympathetic ophthalmia should be suspected in any patient with a history of penetrating globe trauma who present complaining of blurred vision, photophobia, and ocular redness. Clinical findings, which are indistinguishable from those in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, include bilateral panuveitis, mutton fat keratic precipitates, exudative retinal detachments, and focal choroiditis. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrates choroidal thickening.
High-dose oral corticosteroids should be started immediately, but management with immunomodulatory agents is required in most patients. Topical corticosteroids are insufficient to address posterior disease. Intravitreal steroids are not standard of care for this bilateral disease.

Q2845
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What laboratory test would be most helpful in working up a patient whose condition is suspicious for multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis?
Correct answer: B. rapid plasma reagin (RPR)
Rationale
Multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis (MFC) is an idiopathic inflammatory disorder. It presents, mostly in young myopic women, with decreased vision, photopsias, and an enlarged blind spot. While HSV and EBV have been postulated, neither has been proven as causative, and MFC is still considered idiopathic and a diagnosis of exclusion. Because sarcoidosis, syphilis, and tuberculosis can produce lesions similar to those seen in MFC, those conditions should be ruled out through specific testing. Of the tests listed, RPR (and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption [FTA-ABS]) would be most helpful to rule out syphilis, especially before starting steroid therapy.
EBV and HSV have been postulated but not proven to be causative of MFC. B. henselae is associated with cat-scratch disease and is classic for a macular star associated with optic nerve edema.

Q2846
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the primary cause of transient increases in intraocular pressure (IOP) in an eye with acute keratouveitis due to herpes simplex virus (HSV)?
Correct answer: A. trabeculitis
Rationale
Ocular hypertension associated with herpetic uveitis may be a helpful diagnostic hallmark. Most other inflammatory syndromes are associated with decreased intraocular pressure (IOP) that occurs as a result of ciliary body hyposecretion. However, herpesvirus may cause trabeculitis and thus increase IOP, often to as high as 50–60 mm Hg. In addition, inflammatory cells may contribute to trabecular obstruction and congestion.
Appositional angle closure, pupillary block, and increased episcleral venous pressure are not associated with acute HSV infection.

Q2847
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the preferred treatment for diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN)?
Correct answer: B. laser photocoagulation
Rationale
Diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis is a posterior uveitis thought to be caused by a solitary nematode residing and migrating within the subretinal space. The dog hookworm Ancylostoma caninum and the larger raccoon roundworm Baylisascaris procyonis are believed to be the most common causative organisms. The disease features vitritis, optic nerve swelling, and multifocal inflammation of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium. Inflammatory lesions are typically multifocal, gray-white, and approximately 1 disc diameter in size. Occasionally, an s-shaped nematode is visible in the subretinal space. The preferred and most definitive treatment of DUSN is direct photocoagulation of the organism, which can halt further disease progression. Although systemic corticosteroids can treat inflammation, they do not treat the underlying cause. Systemic antihelminthics have had variable reported success. Vitrectomy is not indicated in the treatment of DUSN.

Q2848
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with dense anterior and posterior uveitis and seizures. He had been to India during the past few months. A cranial computed tomography (CT) scan shows a very small calcification and hydrocephalus. A B-scan shows a centrally echo-dense, curvilinear, highly reflective structure superior to the optic nerve. What is the cause of the patient's illness?
Correct answer: D. cysticercosis
Rationale
The B scan structure showing a centrally echo-dense, curvilinear, highly reflective structure superior to the optic nerve is suggestive of the scolex and is characteristic of cysticercosis.
Although the eye is more commonly affected than any other organ, neural cysticercosis is associated with significant morbidity and a mortality of 40%. Epileptiform seizures may be the first sign of cerebral cysticercosis. Both anterior chamber and vitreous may demonstrate inflammatory activity; vitreous inflammation is more pronounced during the early stages of the disease.
Anterior chamber paracentesis may reveal a large number of eosinophils; peripheral eosinophilia may also be present. Anticysticercus antibodies can be detected by ELISA in about 80% of patients with neural cysticercosis.

Q2849
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What time course characterizes recurrent uveitis as defined by the Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group?
Correct answer: A. episodes of uveitis that recur more than 3 months after treatment has been discontinued
Rationale
Episodes of uveitis that recur less than 3 months after treatment has been discontinued are classified as chronic uveitis. Acute uveitis is defined as resolving in fewer than 3 months. The answer choice “episodes of uveitis that recur irrespective of when treatment has been discontinued” is not a currently accepted classification of uveitis. Recurrent uveitis is classified as disease in which patients exhibit periods of quiescence that last longer than 3 months, off of therapy

Q2850
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is a contraindication to cataract surgery in a patient with uveitis?
Correct answer: C. active intraocular inflammation
Rationale
The decision to perform cataract surgery in patients with uveitic eyes differs from considering this surgery for patients with nonuveitic eyes. The potential vision may be subnormal, due to previous macular edema or other permanent ocular damage. Active intraocular inflammation is a strong contraindication for surgery and should only be considered if the risks of delaying surgery outweigh the potential for dramatically exacerbating the inflammation. Complications can be minimized when inflammation has been controlled for several months before surgery and is treated aggressively after surgery.
Steroid-responsive glaucoma is not a contraindication for cataract surgery but should be considered when weighing the relative merits of periocular or intraocular corticosteroid use.
Many uveitis patients require systemic immunomodulatory therapy to obtain the necessary control of the inflammatory process before cataract surgery; the ideal scenario is absence of inflammatory cells, regardless of what specific therapies are required to achieve this state, before proceeding with cataract surgery.

Q2851
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Patients with what ocular inflammatory disorder might benefit from pars plana vitrectomy?
Correct answer: D. intermediate uveitis
Rationale
Vitrectomy can be useful as a diagnostic tool if infectious or neoplastic vitreous infiltration is suspected, and it can also be useful in treating cases of inflammatory intermediate uveitis for visual rehabilitation. Removal of vitreous opacity, epiretinal membranes, repair of retinal detachments, and other primary indications can provide direct benefit, and some authors suggest that it provides better control of inflammation and improvement in cystoid macular edema. Vitrectomy is not reported as efficacious in cases of anterior uveitis, serpiginous chorioretinopathy, or Bartonella neuroretinitis.

Q2852
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Detection of what antibody is most commonly associated with systemic granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
Correct answer: C. anti-proteinase 3
Rationale
The antibody most commonly associated with systemic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is the antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) anti-proteinase 3, also known as c-ANCA.
Ribonucleoproteins are frequently encountered in mixed connective tissue diseases and Sjögren syndrome (SS). In SS, the anti-ribonucleoproteins include anti-SSA and anti-SSB. Anti-dsDNA antibodies can be found in systemic lupus erythematosus. The anti-ENAs are also associated with mixed connective tissue diseases.

Q2853
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What feature characterizes West Nile virus retinopathy?
Correct answer: C. The virus can be transmitted to humans by mosquitoes.
Rationale
West Nile virus is typically transmitted to humans by mosquitoes. Retinopathy is an uncommon manifestation of the disease, which is caused by a single-stranded RNA flavivirus. The bird serves as the primary host. The retinitis is typically bilateral. Although there is no proven treatment, the disease is usually self-limited. The visual prognosis is favorable.

Q2854
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What type of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is associated with the highest risk of developing uveitis?
Correct answer: C. oligoarticular onset
Rationale
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is classified into 5 types according to International League of Associations of Rheumatology (ILAR) guidelines. Oligoarticular onset, also known as pauciarticular onset, accounts for 80%-90% of patients with JIA-associated uveitis. Four or fewer joints are involved in the first 6 months of the disease. Ocular involvement is rare in systemic onset JIA. Polyarticular onset cases account for only 10% of JIA-associated uveitis. Enthesitis-related arthritis (ERA) is associated with a lower risk of uveitis than oligoarticular onset; however, uveitis in ERA patients is more likely to be acute and recurrent.

Q2855
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What useful clinical feature suggests Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome?
Correct answer: A. alopecia and poliosis
Rationale
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome is associated with alopecia, vitiligo, and poliosis in about 30% of affected patients. It is more common in darkly pigmented ethnic groups and typically affects patients 30 to 50 years of age. It is not associated with skin hyperpigmentation. Additional occasionally useful features are headache, stiff neck, and meningismus.

Q2856
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 19-year-old patient with multiple sclerosis presents with floaters and blurred vision in the left eye. What finding is expected on ocular examination?
Correct answer: B. intermediate uveitis
Rationale
Floaters and blurred vision are symptoms of intermediate uveitis, which may be associated with multiple sclerosis. Pain and redness are symptoms of anterior uveitis. Optic neuritis, despite being associated with multiple sclerosis, does not present with floaters.

Q2857
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome experienced resolution of bilateral serous retinal detachments with oral corticosteroid therapy. Six months later, the patient's visual acuity is 20/25 in both eyes. However, despite prednisolone acetate 1% drops every 2 hours and prednisone 20 mg/day orally, the patient is still plagued with persistent active anterior uveitis (2+ cells) in both eyes. What is the best next step in the treatment of this patient's condition?
Correct answer: C. Initiate systemic immunomodulatory therapy.
Rationale
Even though VKH syndrome is usually responsive to corticosteroid therapy, patients may experience recurrent episodes of inflammation. It is not safe nor recommended to use systemic corticosteroids on a long-term basis, so if there is recurrent inflammation, steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy should be considered.
VKH usually causes panuveitis, so topical therapy with corticosteroids will not be adequate.
The diagnosis of VKH is made on primarily clinical findings, so there is little confirmatory information to gain by performing diagnostic vitrectomy in this patient.

Q2858
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What feature is most consistent with uveitis in oligoarticular (also known as pauciarticular) juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA; formerly referred to as juvenile chronic arthritis and juvenile rheumatoid arthritis)?
Correct answer: D. bilateral chronic anterior uveitis
Rationale
Indolent, bilateral, chronic anterior uveitis, characterized by a low-grade anterior chamber cellular reaction, is the most common ocular manifestation of oligoarticular JIA. Other manifestations of JIA-associated, chronic anterior uveitis include fine keratic precipitates, band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, cataracts, glaucoma, and macular edema. Intermediate uveitis with snowbanking is very rare in patients with JIA, and chorioretinal scars typically do not develop in these patients.

Q2859
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What would be the preferred management of a 12-year-old child who demonstrates the findings shown?
Correct answer: D. surgical parasite removal
Rationale
This picture shows intraocular cysticercosis. Antihelminthic drugs can be helpful for neural cysticercosis, and a systemic evaluation is important, but antihelminthic drugs do not penetrate well into the eye. Laser can be helpful for small organisms under the retina, but larger and killed parasites can incite inflammation. The prognosis if untreated is poor, often with phthisis in 3–5 years. Surgical removal is the preferred treatment of this parasite. Antihelminthic medication (including albendazole) is useful for neurocysticercosis, but is not effective for ocular infection.

Q2860
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A pseudophakic 52-year-old man complains of floaters and is found to have anterior chamber flare and cells in the anterior vitreous. He has a laser demarcation around an inferior retinal detachment. What is the most likely cause of his cell and flare?
Correct answer: B. rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
Rationale
Chronic peripheral rhegmatogenous retinal detachment can be associated with anterior segment cell and flare, along with vitreous cells. Patients often have good vision that can sometimes deteriorate because of cystoid macular edema (CME). Careful dilated fundus examination with scleral depression is of paramount importance in establishing the diagnosis. Findings may include peripheral pigment demarcation lines, subretinal fluid, retinal breaks, subretinal fibrosis, and peripheral retinal cysts.
Photoreceptor outer segments liberated from the subretinal space may be present in the anterior chamber, simulating inflammatory cells. In such situations, intraocular pressure (IOP) may be elevated, as these photoreceptor outer segments are phagocytosed by the endothelial cells in the trabecular meshwork, resulting in secondary open-angle glaucoma. This condition is called Schwartz syndrome; however, the condition is rare and specific to very anteriorized tears in the retina, involving the vitreous base, that give shed photoreceptor outer segments access to the anterior chamber (otherwise, with more posterior tears, photoreceptor outer segments would be trapped in the posterior segment by an intact hyaloid face).

Q2861
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What side effect is a known complication of intravitreal ganciclovir injections?
Correct answer: B. retinal detachment
Rationale
A known complication of intravitreal injections (as a whole, not just of ganciclovir) is retinal tear and detachment.
Intravitreal ganciclovir is not known to be associated with optic neuritis.
Although intravitreal injections of ganciclovir can transiently increase intraocular pressure, they are not associated with chronic glaucoma.
In addition to other antivirals (such as foscarnet and valganciclovir) that act on cytomegalovirus (CMV), the use of intravitreal ganciclovir may actually decrease the incidence of immune recovery uveitis, as opposed to promoting it. The exception to this rule is cidofovir, in which case the probability that a patient will develop immune recovery uveitis is significantly greater than in patients never having received this particular antiviral agent.
Additionally, 50% of patients with CMV retinitis and many other cases of viral retinitis may develop a retinal detachment during active disease or after successful treatment. Due to friability from retinal necrosis and multiple posterior holes, long-term silicone tamponade is often needed for surgical repair.

Q2862
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
When testing a patient with a suspected sarcoidosis, what invasive evaluation has the lowest yield (sensitivity) of confirming a diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. biopsy of normal-appearing conjunctiva
Rationale
The most sensitive tests for detecting sarcoidosis are biopsy of a clinically apparent granuloma and computed tomography (CT) of the chest. However, biopsy of normal-appearing conjunctiva is very low yield.
In patients with suggestive chest imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage, and biopsy can be diagnostic, with a sensitivity approaching 90% for ultrasound-guided biopsy of pulmonary granulomas. Gallium scans may increase the sensitivity over plain chest radiography, but interpretation usually requires other confirmatory tests.

Q2863
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient with chronic anterior uveitis that is well controlled on topical prednisolone acetate 1% 4 times a day is found to have an intraocular pressure of 24 mm Hg in both eyes. There are 270 degrees of posterior synechiae. On gonioscopy, the angle is open. The optic nerve heads are without glaucomatous change. What is the next step in the management of this patient's condition?
Correct answer: D. an attempt to taper topical corticosteroids
Rationale
This patient has increased intraocular pressure due to use of topical corticosteroids. The angle is open without evidence of peripheral anterior synechiae, and there is no pupil block, so peripheral iridotomy is not indicated. Argon laser trabeculoplasty is usually not performed in uveitic glaucomas, in order to avoid exacerbating the uveitis.
Systemic immunosuppression with methotrexate can be offered if the topical steroids are ineffective. Uveitis is corticosteroid dependent and recurs every time corticosteroids are tapered, as well as if there are complications such as cystoid macular edema and secondary glaucoma.
In this situation, the topical corticosteroids can be gradually tapered, and in the meantime, topical anti–ocular-hypertensive agents can be employed if the raised intraocular pressure seems likely to cause harm. (It is doubtful in this case, because of non-glaucomatous optic nerves and mildly high IOP.)

Q2864
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 40-year-old man complains of painless, progressive blurring of vision in one eye. Examination reveals a low-grade iritis, diffuse iris transillumination without posterior synechiae, and a 3+ posterior subcapsular cataract. There are diffuse stellate keratic precipitates. What is the best choice of preoperative treatment for cataract surgery in this patient?
Correct answer: B. No preoperative treatment is needed.
Rationale
Fuchs uveitis syndrome (sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is unilateral, and symptoms can be overlooked. Blurry vision and discomfort are reported. Typically, patients have diffuse iris stromal atrophy leading to heterochromia, diffuse white stellate keratic precipitates, anterior chamber and anterior vitreous cells, or cataract. The diagnosis is usually based on heterochromia, distribution of the keratic precipitates, lack of posterior synechiae, and lack of symptoms.
The prognosis is good in most cases, although the inflammation can linger for years. Topical steroids can alleviate the inflammation, but typically do not resolve it. Aggressive treatment is not indicated in most of the cases.
These patients do quite well with cataract surgery and generally no preoperative treatment is needed.

Q2865
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 78-year-old pseudophakic man from a nursing home presented with severe pain and visual acuity of 20/100. He was diagnosed with endophthalmitis with culture showing streptococcal species. What part of this history portends a good prognosis?
Correct answer: B. relatively good visual acuity at presentation
Rationale
Severe cases of endophthalmitis are correlated with loss of red fundus reflex, afferent pupillary defect, and poor vision at the time of initial presentation.
Lens status and living condition are not significant risk prognosticators.

Q2866
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 27-year-old woman has bilateral panuveitis, cavitary lung lesions, and kidney failure. What prophylactic measures should be considered before initiating definitive therapy with the most effective immunomodulatory treatment for this condition?
Correct answer: C. oocyte harvest and banking
Rationale
The patient in this clinical scenario has granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Of GPA patients treated with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids, 93% successfully achieve remission.
Oocyte harvest and banking is prudent in a patient about to start cyclophosphamide who plans future pregnancies. Cyclophosphamide interferes with oogenesis and spermatogenesis. It may cause sterility in both sexes, and in some patients this may be irreversible. Other well-established adverse effects include teratogenicity, hemorrhagic cystitis, and development of secondary malignancies.
Variants in the gene encoding thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) alter its activity and may contribute to increased risk of hematologic events or leukopenia in treatment with thiopurines (eg, azathioprine), not cyclophosphamide.
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan/bone densitometry detects osteopenia/osteoporosis. It is useful in long-term corticosteroid administration, but osteopenia is not a significant risk of cyclophosphamide use.
Transesophageal echocardiogram detects cardiac and valvular structural abnormalities. Cardiac valve disease is not a significant risk of cyclophosphamide use, although acute cardiotoxicity has been reported in the setting of antineoplastic multi-drug therapy and transplant procedures involving this drug.

Q2867
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is a recommended therapy for Lyme disease?
Correct answer: D. doxycycline
Rationale
Doxycycline, ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, and cefuroxime are recommended when antibiotic treatment of Lyme disease is necessary. There is currently no FDA-approved vaccine for Lyme disease in the United States. Atovaquone is an anti-parasitic drug that is not used for Lyme disease.

Q2868
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Cyclosporine has been proven effective in controlled clinical studies for the treatment of what ocular inflammatory disease?
Correct answer: A. Behçet disease-related uveitis
Rationale
Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor that eliminates T-cell receptor signal transduction, down-regulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4+ T-lymphocytes. Cyclosporine has been shown to be effective in treating Behçet disease-associated uveitis in a randomized, controlled clinical trial; it provided control of inflammation in 50% of patients.
APMPPE usually does not require treatment; it is self-limited most of the time.
Immune recovery uveitis is anterior or intermediate uveitis, which presents when immune status improves with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Usually, immune recovery uveitis is treated with local steroid therapy; systemic immunosuppressants are not indicated.
An infectious etiology should be ruled out in postsurgical scleritis before systemic immunosuppressants are used.

Q2869
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most appropriate treatment for  Lyme disease with papillitis?
Correct answer: D. intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone for 2 weeks
Rationale
Stage 2, or disseminated, Lyme disease occurs a few weeks after exposure to spirochetes. The spirochetes spread to the skin, central nervous system (CNS), joints, heart, and eyes. The ocular disease in stage 2 includes anterior uveitis, intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis, and panuveitis. These can be associated with granulomatous anterior uveitis, papillitis, choroiditis, vasculitis, and exudative retinal detachment.
Intraocular inflammation associated with Lyme disease, just like syphilis, is regarded as a manifestation of CNS disease. Patients require systemic (with oral amoxicillin or doxycycline; or intravenous ceftriaxone) antibiotic therapy. The routine use of systemic corticosteroids is still controversial, as antibiotic failures have been reported when corticosteroids are employed.
If corticosteroids are to be used to avoid a Jarisch-Herxheimer–like reaction, then oral (instead of intravenous) corticosteroids can be considered.

Q2870
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What form of uveitis is most likely to last less than 1 week?
Correct answer: C. Posner-Schlossman syndrome
Rationale
Glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome) is characterized by recurrent unilateral hypertensive nongranulomatous anterior uveitis. This type of uveitis typically lasts less than 1 week. The other conditions listed are characterized by inflammation that lasts for longer than a week.

Q2871
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What should be the initial treatment of neovascularization of the disc in a patient with sarcoid-related panuveitis?
Correct answer: C. corticosteroid and immunomodulatory treatment
Rationale
Retinal neovascularization in uveitis results from chronic inflammation or capillary nonperfusion. Sarcoid panuveitis may be complicated with neovascularization of the disc and resolves completely with immunomodulatory and corticosteroid therapy alone.
Uveitides with retinal vasculitis may cause retinal neovascularization due to ischemia and thus may necessitate retinal laser photocoagulation or intravitreal anti-VEGF injection.
Treatment of subfoveal choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is accomplished with VEGF inhibitors; photodynamic therapy with verteporfin may be an adjunctive treatment.
In all cases, however, control of inflammation is paramount; this also reduces the risk of recurrence of CNV.

Q2872
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What antimetabolite is most commonly associated with hepatic toxicity?
Correct answer: D. methotrexate
Rationale
Although any antimetabolite can be associated with hepatic toxicity, methotrexate is most commonly associated with it. Often the elevation of liver enzyme levels is modest and reversible on holding the medication or decreasing the dose. Rarely, the liver damage can be severe and persistent, with resultant significant morbidity. Reversible hepatic toxicity occurs in 15% of patients on methotrexate, as opposed to 2% of patients taking azathioprine. Toxicity associated with azathioprine can be mitigated by assessing for thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) activity.

Q2873
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What percentage of all blindness in the United States is attributed to inadequately treated uveitis?
Correct answer: D. 10%
Rationale
Worldwide, ocular inflammatory disease is a significant cause of low vision and blindness. In the United States, 10% of all blindness is attributed to inadequately treated uveitis.

Q2874
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Three weeks ago, a 78-year-old man tripped and fell on a sidewalk and his right eye was perforated by the tooth of a rake. He has a 360-degree dense subconjunctival hemorrhage, an intraocular pressure of 8, and a peaked pupil. The left eye has the appearance shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. sympathetic ophthalmia
Rationale
The attached photo is significant for granulomatous keratic precipitates. Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous uveitis that occurs after trauma to one of the eyes. A septic endophthalmitis would not be expected in the nontraumatized eye. Sarcoidosis and Lyme disease can also cause granulomatous uveitis, though those diagnoses are less likely in this scenario.

Q2875
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient with AIDS presents with bilateral yellow, placoid retinal lesions. What is the best initial testing to perform and best initial treatment?
Correct answer: D. Check rapid plasmin reagin and start intravenous penicillin G, 18-24 million U, administered daily for 10 days.
Rationale
Syphilis may occur as a coinfection in HIV-affected individuals. Syphilis in such patients may present as placoid lesions, as described in this case. Thus, suspicion for syphilis should be high in this patient and checking the rapid plasmin reagin (RPR) will help assess response to treatment. Ocular cases of syphilis should be treated in the same manner as neurosyphilis. Thus, intravenous penicillin G 18-24 million units for 10-14 days is indicated. Syphilis without neurologic or ocular involvement may be treated intramuscularly as a single dose.
Checking CD4+ helper T lymphocyte count and starting antiretroviral therapy would be an ideal option if the patient exhibited features only of HIV retinopathy (cotton-wool spots, microaneurysms, and retinal hemorrhages). Systemic corticosteroids may be used in treating immune recovery uveitis, which occurs in the setting of prior CMV retinitis. However, systemic steroids may be used if there is a prominent inflammatory reaction in syphilis. The use of systemic steroids, however, should only occur after treatment with intravenous penicillin has commenced.

Q2876
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What dosage of oral prednisone is considered to be the threshold for increasing toxicity that can induce osteoporosis?
Correct answer: C. 7.5 mg
Rationale
The risk of osteoporosis is higher for postmenopausal women and men older than 50 years who take ≥7.5 mg/day of prednisone or its equivalent for longer than 3 months. To lessen the risk, patients receiving long-term corticosteroid maintenance therapy should supplement their diets with calcium and vitamin D, except with certain medications; the advice of the physician prescribing those drugs should be obtained.

Q2877
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient presents with acute anterior uveitis and decreased vision. The patient denies pain with eye movements. Pupillary function is normal without afferent pupillary defect. Color plates are full. Anterior segment findings include 2+ diffuse perilimbal injection, 3+ anterior chamber cell, 1+ flare, and a clear crystalline lens. Dilated fundoscopic examination shows hyperemia of the optic nerve and a blunted foveal reflex, but no vitritis or chorioretinal lesions. What test would most likely demonstrate the cause of decreased vision in this case?
Correct answer: A. optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula
Rationale
The cause of the patient's decreased vision would best be discerned through OCT of the macula, as it is not uncommon for inflammatory cytokines associated with acute anterior uveitis to diffuse posteriorly and result in swelling of the optic nerve head and in cystoid macular edema (CME).
It is important to understand that the presence of optic nerve and retinal edema alone are not synonymous with posterior uveitis or optic neuritis. Optic nerve and retinal edema occur in many processes including anterior uveitis, intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis, panuveitis. Edema can also occur in unrelated entities such as hypotony maculopathy in the setting of an overfiltering bleb in glaucoma patients. To further clarify that the optic nerve head hyperemia in this patient is not indicative of an optic neuritis or posterior uveitis, the question stem not only states that this is an acute anterior uveitis, but also explains that there is no pain with eye movements, no vitritis, no chorioretinitis, no afferent pupillary defect, and full color plate testing. Another option to ensure that optic nerve function is normal could be to perform a visual field, which should either be full in the absence of other pathology or show a possible enlarged blind spot from the edema at the nerve head. Therefore, OCT and/or B-scan ultrasonography of the optic nerve head will not be as helpful in this scenario, as there is no reason to suspect an optic neuritis or posterior scleritis with associated optic nerve swelling in this case.
ERG may be helpful in conditions primarily involving the retina or choroid, such as certain white dot syndromes or birdshot retinochoroidopathy, but not in the setting of acute anterior uveitis where optic nerve head edema and macular edema can result from posterior diffusion of inflammatory cytokines.
