Q2878
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What symptom(s) characterize(s) the presentation of serpiginous choroiditis?
Correct answer: D. sudden onset of central or paracentral scotoma
Rationale
Serpiginous choroiditis, also termed geographic or helicoid choroidopathy, is likely inflammatory, but it typically does not manifest with significant vitreous or anterior segment inflammation. Because of this, floaters and photophobia are not cardinal symptoms. The onset of symptoms is relatively sudden with a painless, unilateral, paracentral scotoma and potentially decreased vision, but it may proceed asymmetrically and with intermittent periods of progression. Many patients progress to vision of 20/200 or worse with involvement of the macula, but this decline in visual acuity typically develops over months or years. Patients may require aggressive anti-inflammatory treatment and need to be followed closely for the development of choroidal neovascularization and progression of disease. Tuberculosis-associated disease should be considered in the differential diagnosis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2879
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What test is most appropriate in the initial workup of a patient with uveitis suspected of having sarcoidosis?
Correct answer: B. chest x-ray
Rationale
Chest x-ray is the single best screening modality for patients suspected of having sarcoidosis, as it reveals abnormalities in approximately 90% of patients who have sarcoidosis. The classic feature of a chest x-ray (CXR) in this setting is hilar lymphadenopathy, although chest computed tomography (CT) may also reveal mediastinal and other parenchymal abnormalities. Although retinal angiography may reveal leakage from retinal vasculitis (technically, retinal phlebitis), retinal vasculitis is not specific to sarcoidosis and can be seen in several other posterior uveitides. ANA and CRP have no screening value for patients suspected of having sarcoidosis.
Chest abnormalities are present at some point in up to 90% of sarcoid patients, but these do not persist throughout the disease course and thus maybe absent at the time of workup. High resolution chest computed tomography is more sensitive imaging modality and may be particularly valuable in patients with a normal appearance on CXR, but for whom a high clinical index of suspicion remains; the risk of increased radiation must be weighed against the clinical utility of the information gained in such cases.

Q2880
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most effective treatment for preventing sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) in the fellow eye after a penetrating trauma that resulted in "no light perception" vision in the traumatized eye?
Correct answer: D. enucleation of the traumatized eye
Rationale
SO is a bilateral, granulomatous panuveitis that may develop after trauma or surgery in 1 eye. After a latency period, the uninjured fellow eye (sympathizing eye) develops panuveitis. Until recently, accidental penetrating ocular trauma was the most common precipitating event. Vitreoretinal surgery has now become the main risk for developing SO.
Every attempt should be made to repair the injury and close the ocular wounds, as soon as possible. However, if the eye is grossly disorganized, with no possible salvage, then enucleation within 2 weeks of injury may prevent the development of SO.
Systemic steroids and immunosuppressive therapy are indicated for the initial treatment of SO once the condition is present. However, prophylactic steroids and immunosuppressive therapy have not been shown to prevent the development of SO.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2881
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What systemic medical condition is associated with acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)?
Correct answer: C. cerebral vasculitis
Rationale
Although APMPPE typically occurs in otherwise healthy adults, systemic conditions should be considered. Cerebral vasculitis can be a complicating comorbid condition, and syphilis may masquerade with an indistinguishable fundus appearance.
Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common autoimmune disease associated with scleritis or peripheral ulcerative keratitis.
MS has been associated with many types of ocular inflammation but optic neuritis and intermediate uveitis are most typical.
Central nervous system lymphoma may present with intraocular lymphoma; the subretinal and vitreous aggregates of lymphoid cells may share features of APMPPE at first, but typically affect much older patients, and are progressive—both uncharacteristic of APMPPE.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2882
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For a patient less than 6 years old with unilateral pseudohypopyon, what is the primary concern when considering an aqueous or vitreous aspirate?
Correct answer: C. risk of dispersing malignant retinoblastoma cells
Rationale
Retinoblastoma, especially the variant of diffuse infiltrating retinoblastoma, may present with anterior chamber cells, pseudohypopyon that shifts with change of head position, or vitreous opacity and other signs of inflammation, but lack the typical calcification usually seen with this tumor. Aspiration can be diagnostic, but it carries the risk of seeding the tumor via the needle or surgical track. The risks of general anesthesia and direct complications of diagnostic aspiration, such as cataract formation and sympathetic ophthalmia, are low; thus, if definitive diagnosis and subsequent management necessitates obtaining an aspirate, benefits would outweigh risks.

Q2883
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 52-year-old white woman presents with decreased vision. The fundoscopic examination image is shown. What treatment should be initiated?
Correct answer: D. systemic and/or local corticosteroids with early introduction of corticosteroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy
Rationale
The fundus photos show birdshot retinochoroidopathy (vitiliginous chorioretinitis). This is a relatively uncommon disease that is classically found in white women of northern European descent, 40 years and older. There is no known systemic association with this disease. Birdshot retinochoroidopathy has a high correlation with the HLA-A29 haplotype, which has a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 93%, according to the Basic and Clinical Science Course. The fundoscopic examination of birdshot retinochoroidopathy shows characteristic multifocal, hypopigmented, ovoid, cream-colored lesions at the level of the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Patients present with decreased vision, nyctalopia, floaters, or disturbed color vision. Electroretinography and visual field testing are useful in following disease course and response to therapy. Without treatment, few patients maintain good vision.
Typical treatment consists initially of systemic corticosteroids, with immunomodulatory medications for adjunct and maintenance therapy (methotrexate, cyclosporine, etc.). Periocular steroid can also be useful in treatment for cystoid macular edema (CME), on the complications of birdshot retinochoroidopathy.
Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol are used to treat tuberculosis, which may mimic a serpiginous choroiditis. Intravitreal ganciclovir may be used to treat herpes simplex virus-associated chorioretinitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2884
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A positive result on an indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for Borrelia burgdorferi in a patient with intermediate uveitis should prompt what action as the most appropriate next step?
Correct answer: A. confirmation of serological results with a Western blot
Rationale
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends a 2-step protocol for the diagnosis of active or previous infection with Borrelia burgdorferi: ELISA for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and IgG, and if this result is positive, then Western immunoblot testing.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based testing can also be used.
For patients with only ocular involvement (ie, without CNS or cardiac involvement), the route and duration of antibiotic treatment is not well established.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2885
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What animal model of uveitis most closely resembles Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome in humans?
Correct answer: B. experimental autoimmune uveoretinitis
Rationale
VKH is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis in humans. Of the choices listed, only experimental autoimmune uveoretinitis induces a panuveitis. Equine recurrent uveitis can produce vitreal involvement, but it is mainly an anterior uveitis. AIRE (for autoimmune regulator) is a transcription factor used by the thymus in the process of establishing thymic tolerance. Early in life, the thymus expresses many cell-type–specific proteins; T‑cell clones reactive to these proteins are deleted. This mechanism is important in the development of self-tolerance. Mice deficient in AIRE do not express these proteins during development; thus, autoreactive T cells escape deletion, and the mice spontaneously develop a posterior uveitis. Endotoxin-induced (also termed experimental immune) uveitis (EIU) is a transient uveitis model induced by footpad, intraperitoneal, or intravitreal injection of lipopolysaccharide in mice and rats.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2886
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most appropriate indication for chorioretinal biopsy?
Correct answer: D. sight-threatening chorioretinitis with negative workup that is nonresponsive to therapy
Rationale
When diagnostic workup, as in the case of sight-threatening chorioretinitis, fails to reveal a diagnosis or, at the very least distinguish between noninfectious, infectious, or masquerade (eg, malignant) etiologies, a chorioretinal biopsy can be considered, since this will biopsy the tissue directly involved.
In the case of a diffuse unilateral vitritis in a 4-year-old child, vitreous aspiration or vitrectomy is more appropriate, especially considering that this is the primary site of involvement. The case of bilateral heavy vitritis with subretinal infiltrates is suspicious for a masquerade syndrome (namely primary vitreoretinal lymphoma), and in such cases a vitrectomy can be both diagnostic and therapeutic. Ancillary tests could be considered in such cases, and assays for IL-10 and IL-6 levels (from vitreous or aqueous) could be included.
An acute, diffuse, unilateral peripheral retinal whitening with vascular sheathing is consistent with acute retinal necrosis. In this setting, vitreous (or aqueous) aspiration should be considered to evaluate for herpetic etiologies (including herpes simplex virus [HSV]-1/2, varicella zoster virus [VZV], or, in immunocompromised patients, cytomegalovirus [CMV]) via polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2887
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the typical ophthalmoscopic finding in multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis?
Correct answer: D. small creamy lesions acutely that become punched out over time
Rationale
The inflammatory lesions in multifocal choroiditis may vary somewhat in number, appearance, and location, but they are rarely larger than 1500 μm, evolve into punched-out atrophic scars, and are associated with at least some degree of vitreous and sometimes anterior chamber inflammation. The lesions associated with birdshot retinochoroidopathy are often arranged in a radiating pattern centered on the optic nerve.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2888
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
When stellate keratic precipitates are present in herpes simplex type 1 intraocular infections, how are they typically distributed on the corneal endothelium?
Correct answer: B. diffusely
Rationale
Stellate keratic precipitates (KPs) are very suggestive of a viral intraocular infection and are frequently seen. However, in herpetic intraocular infections, particularly with herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2 as well as varicella-zoster virus, there may be nongranulomatous or granulomatous KPs as well. In this question, stellate KPs are identified and, when present, often are found diffusely. The KPs localizing only to the inferior third of the cornea (Arlt triangle) are classically found in noninfectious etiologies of intraocular inflammation and may be either granulomatous or nongranulomatous. Coin-shaped lesions are found in cytomegalovirus anterior uveitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2889
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
At a minimum, most uveitis specialists will employ what study in the workup of ocular inflammation in an immunocompetent patient?
Correct answer: B. syphilis serology
Rationale
There is no single, standardized battery of tests to be ordered for all patients with uveitis. It is important to rule out an underlying systemic or infectious disease. At a minimum, it might be worthwhile to order a few tests based on the assessment of uveitis questionnaire.
Complementary investigations for uveitis should be guided by a pretest probability of etiology, the ophthalmic signs and symptoms, and therapeutic consequences.
Syphilis is one of great masqueraders of medicine and should always be considered in the differential diagnosis of any intraocular inflammatory disease.
The prevalence of lupus is less than 0.47% in patients with uveitis, so the positive predictive value of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) for the diagnosis is less than 3%. Therefore, checking ANA titers is rarely useful.
ESR and C-reactive protein are nonspecific, so are rarely helpful in finding an etiology.
Tests for tuberculosis are routinely considered in the "essential" workup; however, if an immunocompetent patient with uveitis is from an area where tuberculosis is not endemic, has a reliable travel history, and has had no exposure to other people with tuberculosis, TB testing would have a low yield.
An HLA-B27 should be considered for patients in the pertinent demographic and who have an appropriate presentation, but HLA-B27 would not be the first choice for a "minimal" workup.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2890
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For patients in the early course of birdshot retinochoroidopathy, what is the most common cause of decreased central visual acuity?
Correct answer: A. cystoid macular edema (CME)
Rationale
Vitreous opacities, cataract, RPE atrophy, and CME can characterize birdshot retinochoroidopathy. However, CME is the most common cause of decreased central visual acuity in birdshot, with one study noting 50.5% of cases having CME as the most common cause of visual loss. Recall that CME is the most frequent cause of vision loss in general in uveitic patients. Cataract would be expected to develop either if the inflammation is not controlled or if frequent and chronic topical, periocular, or high-dose systemic corticosteroids are employed. Vitreous haze can develop in birdshot, though it is rarely significant enough to affect visual acuity. RPE atrophy, in addition to optic nerve pallor and vascular attenuation, is a late manifestation of the disease.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2891
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A new patient presents for assessment of uveitis with a calcific band in the interpalpebral zone. What does that tell you about the patient's uveitis?
Correct answer: D. It is chronic.
Rationale
Calcific band keratopathy develops in patients with chronic uveitis over years. It is not specifically associated with sarcoidosis or anterior uveitis and is not painful.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2892
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the causative organism of iris gummas?
Correct answer: C. Treponema pallidum
Rationale
Treponema pallidum

Gummas (or gummata) are the characteristic lesions of benign tertiary syphilis. The ocular manifestations of syphilis are protean and may affect all structures in the eye. Syphilitic iridocyclitis may be associated with iris roseola, iris papulosa, iris nodosa, and iris gummata. Syphilis is a spirochete infection caused by Treponema pallidum.
Baylisascaris procyonis is a raccoon roundworm causing diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease, and Bartonella henselae is the causative agent of cat-scratch disease.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2893
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most common cause of vision loss due to ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS)?
Correct answer: B. choroidal neovascularization (CNV)
Rationale
The most common cause of vision loss in OHS is CNV. If 1 eye with OHS has CNV, then the risk that the other eye will develop visual loss is 1% if there are no findings of OHS in the fellow eye; 4% if there is peripapillary atrophy in the fellow eye; and 25% if focal macular histo spots are present. The treatment of CNV in OHS includes photodynamic therapy or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy.
Inflammatory vitreous opacities and retinal vasculitis are absent in OHS. The classic peripheral punched-out chorioretinal scars of OHS typically do not cause vision loss.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2894
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For an AIDS patient that has the fundus findings shown, what is the most likely symptom that he might experience?
Correct answer: C. no symptoms (asymptomatic)
Rationale
The image represents peripheral "granular" cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Typical features include minimal or no vitreous inflammation, preservation of the vessels (although varying amounts of vasculitis/sheathing may be present), and steady progression without treatment. Because the lesions are usually peripheral and the host immune response is compromised, signs or symptoms such as pain, redness, and decreased vision are scarce; thus, routine screening ophthalmoscopy is recommended for those with CD4+ T-cell counts below 250 cells/μL.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2895
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 32-year-old woman reports one week of floaters in her left eye. She denies flashes of light or sudden trauma. On examination, the ophthalmologist notices a mild anterior chamber reaction and peripheral snowballs and snowbanks in the affected eye. What tests would be most appropriate to order?
Correct answer: B. Lyme titers, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and rapid plasma reagin (RPR)
Rationale
The findings noted suggest pars planitis. The differential diagnosis for this includes sarcoidosis, syphilis, toxocariasis, lyme disease, multiple sclerosis, and tuberculosis. Toxoplasmosis does not cause pars planitis, nor does HLA-B27-associated uveitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2896
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
In what part of the eye does endogenous fungal endophthalmitis typically begin?
Correct answer: D. choroid
Rationale
The infection usually begins in the choroid, appearing as yellow-white lesions with indistinct borders that range in size from small cotton-wool spots to several disc diameters. It can subsequently break through into the vitreous, producing localized cellular and fungal aggregates overlying the original site. Iris nodules and rubeosis may also be observed in cases of severe fungal endophthalmitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2897
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Progressive outer retinal necrosis may be distinguished from acute retinal necrosis by the presence of what feature?
Correct answer: D. host immunosuppression
Rationale
The essential difference between progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) and acute retinal necrosis (ARN) is the presence of an intact immune function in ARN. Both PORN and ARN are typically caused by herpes family viruses, specifically herpes simplex types 1 and 2, and the herpes zoster or varicella virus. Goldmann-Witmer coefficient together with PCR increase the yield of diagnosing viral infections. The HLA-A29 genotype is associated with birdshot chorioretinopathy, and has not been reported in relation to viral retinitis. While HLA Aw33 phenotype has been reported to increase the relative risk of developing ARN in Japanese patients.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2898
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Three weeks after bowel surgery, a patient presents with 2+ anterior chamber cells, 2+ vitreous cells, vitreal haze with snowball-like condensations, and a small white retinal lesion in 1 eye. He had been in the intensive care unit on parenteral nutrition for a week. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. Candida albicans endophthalmitis
Rationale
Candida albicans endophthalmitis

Patients receiving parenteral nutrition are at risk for developing fungal infections that can become hematogenously disseminated, thereby resulting in Candida endophthalmitis. Candida is the most common organism causing endogenous endophthalmitis. Candida endophthalmitis will typically present as fluffy, round vitreous opacities in addition to creamy white chorioretinal lesions.
IBD with uveitis typically presents in a patient with IBD symptoms, and this noninfectious uveitis typically presents in a recurrent nongranulomatous manner.
The ocular inflammation in sarcoidosis may present as a granulomatous uveitis and can affect anterior, intermediate, or posterior segments, or be panuveitic in nature.
The classic features of ocular sarcoidosis include mutton-fat keratic precipitates (KPs), Busacca and Koeppe nodules, vitreous snowballs (string of pearls presentation is characteristic), "candlewax dripping" vasculitis, and choroidal and optic nerve nodules (which have been shown to represent granulomas).
The uveitis caused by Tropheryma whipplei can present as panuveitis or retinal vasculitis; this entity should be suspected in patients with abdominal pain, diarrhea or steatorrhea, weight loss, and neurologic dysfunction.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2899
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What intraocular infection is most commonly associated with immune recovery uveitis in a patient with AIDS whose immune function has improved with antiretroviral therapy?
Correct answer: B. cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis
Rationale
Immune recovery uveitis is observed in patients with previous CMV retinitis and recovered immune systems, most often in patients with AIDS who have received antiretroviral therapy. CMV retinitis is usually associated with a minimal inflammatory response in AIDS patients; the inflammation of immune recovery uveitis is presumably the reconstituted immune system’s response to CMV antigens.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2900
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) syndrome is most commonly associated with what virus?
Correct answer: A. varicella-zoster virus (VZV)
Rationale
PORN syndrome is a variant of herpetic viral retinitis seen in HIV-infected patients. Initially, PORN may be difficult to differentiate from CMV retinitis, but rapid progression distinguishes varicella-zoster or herpes simplex from CMV infections.
Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis can mimic PORN in AIDS patients, and vitreous polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is often required to differentiate the possible etiologies.
Bartonella species may cause bacillary angiomatosis or neuroretinitis but are not associated with a peripheral retinitis.
The human papillomavirus (HPV) is associated with cervical and squamous carcinoma but has no known association with retinitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2901
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What neurological complication is most commonly seen with Borrelia burgdorferi infection?
Correct answer: D. seventh cranial nerve palsy
Rationale
The most common neuro-ophthalmologic manifestation of Lyme disease is seventh cranial nerve palsy (Bell palsy). It may be unilateral or bilateral. Other cranial nerve palsies have been reported, and Horner syndrome may be associated but is uncommon. Optic nerve swelling (papillitis) and neuroretinitis are also associated with Lyme disease.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2902
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Histoplasma capsulatum infection most commonly occurs in what geographic area?
Correct answer: B. Ohio and Mississippi River valleys
Rationale
The highest prevalence of H capsulatum exposure is in the Mississippi and Ohio River watersheds. Although the Missouri River is a branch of the Mississippi, H capsulatum has not been found endemic to its valley. Coccidioidomycosis, which can be found in the San Joaquin Valley as well as in the soil of several southwestern states, Mexico, and Central and South America, may mimic the clinical features of presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome ("punched-out" small chorioretinal scars, peripapillary scarring). This disorder is due to the fungus Coccidioides, not H capsulatum. The Hudson River valley is devoid of H capsulatum.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2903
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the definitive treatment for a patient with phacolytic uveitis?
Correct answer: C. cataract surgery
Rationale
An immune reaction to lens material may result in ocular inflammatory disease. This reaction may follow disruption of the lens capsule (traumatic or surgical), termed phacoantigenic uveitis, or leakage of lens protein through the intact lens capsule in mature or hypermature cataracts, termed phacolytic uveitis. While antiinflammatory medications may be used to reduce inflammation, the definitive treatment is to remove the inciting lens material.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2904
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Methotrexate produces its anti-inflammatory effect by what mechanism of action?
Correct answer: C. extracellular release of adenosine
Rationale
Methotrexate, a folic acid analogue and inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, inhibits DNA replication, but its anti-inflammatory effects result from extracellular release of adenosine.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2905
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the treatment for visually significant calcific band keratopathy?
Correct answer: A. epithelial debridement and chelation
Rationale
Not all band keratopathy needs to be treated, but if it is symptomatic or visually significant, the treatment is epithelial debridement followed by chelation with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA).
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2906
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What disease is typically treated with an intravitreal antiviral medication?
Correct answer: A. acute retinal necrosis (ARN) syndrome
Rationale
Acute retinal necrosis is a kind of necrotizing herpetic retinopathy. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based assays have shown that the most common cause of ARN is varicella zoster virus (VZV), followed by herpes simplex virus (HSV)-1, HSV-2, and rarely cytomegalovirus (CMV). High-dose systemic oral or intravenous antiviral therapy alone or in combination with intravitreal antivirals is indicated for treatment of this sight-threatening condition.
An infectious cause has not been proven for MEWDS, Behçet disease, nor VKH, so antivirals are not usually employed for those conditions. 
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2907
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What test is indicated periodically in patients being treated with azathioprine for eye disease with no systemic symptoms?
Correct answer: A. alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
Rationale
Azathioprine is an oral antimetabolite that is often used to treat ocular inflammatory diseases, such as uveitis and mucous membrane pemphigoid. Hepatotoxicity and blood cell dyscrasias are the most common adverse effects that would be detected by screening laboratory studies; thus, most surveillance regimens include getting a complete blood cell count. Liver enzymes, such as ALT, should be checked before initiating therapy, within 1 to 2 weeks after initiating therapy, and regularly thereafter.
Use of the alkylating agent cyclophosphamide can result in hemorrhagic cystitis. Consumption of adequate water is therefore recommended when taking this drug, and urinalysis is indicated. Cyclosporine and tacrolimus are more typically associated with nephrotoxicity, and screening blood pressure measurements and serum creatinine are indicated.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2908
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What medication is best used as an intravitreal injection in the treatment of cytomegalovirus retinitis?
Correct answer: C. foscarnet
Rationale
Foscarnet and ganciclovir are medications appropriate as intravitreal preparations for the treatment of CMV retinitis. Of the choices listed here, foscarnet is the best. Valganciclovir is the L-valyl ester prodrug of ganciclovir. The valine increases both the absorption of the drug in the intestines and the bioavailability of the drug once it is absorbed. Cidofovir was previously used as intravitreal therapy for the treatment of CMV, especially in the pre-highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) era, but this medication is associated with hypotonous uveitis, which can lead to blindness. Acyclovir is not appropriate for CMV, because acyclovir needs to be phosphorylated by a viral thymidine kinase (TK) and CMV lacks TK
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2909
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What infectious organism is mostly likely to cause chorioretinitis adjacent to a chorioretinal scar?
Correct answer: A. toxoplasmosis
Rationale
The most common cause of chorioretinitis is toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasmosis often recurs adjacent to scars indicating a prior episode, but it can also occur at "de novo" locations in the fundus. Acute retinal necrosis (usually secondary to herpes simplex virus or varicella zoster virus) and cytomegalovirus retinitis are not likely to be associated with pre-existing scars. Congenital rubella syndrome may cause diffuse retinal pigment epithelial mottling but is not classically associated with a pre-existing chorioretinal scar.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2910
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
An 18-year-old woman presents with floaters and decreased vision in both eyes. Examination reveals vitreous cells, snowbanking, and cystoid macular edema OU. What systemic disease is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
Correct answer: A. multiple sclerosis
Rationale
Multiple sclerosis is known to develop in 15% of young patients who present with idiopathic intermediate uveitis (pars planitis). CNS lymphoma is largely a disease of the elderly and should be considered in elderly patients who present with idiopathic vitritis. Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive phytanic acid storage disease that presents with a pigmentary retinopathy and reduced electroretinogram (ERG) signals, cerebellar ataxia, polyneuropathy, anosmia, hearing loss, and cardiomyopathy, but not vitritis or intermediate uveitis. Sarcoidosis can masquerade as any form of uveitis but is characterized as a granulomatous anterior or panuveitis rather than an isolated intermediate uveitis.

Q2911
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A patient has parotitis, fever, facial nerve palsy, and uveitis. What disease is the patient most likely to have?
Correct answer: A. sarcoidosis
Rationale
Systemic sarcoidosis may present acutely, frequently with associated anterior uveitis in young patients. One form of acute sarcoidosis, called Löfgren syndrome, consists of erythema nodosum, febrile arthropathy, bilateral hilar adenopathy, and acute iritis and is quite responsive to systemic corticosteroids; it has a good long-term prognosis. Another, termed Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever), is characterized by uveitis, parotitis, fever, and facial nerve palsy. Chronic sarcoidosis presents insidiously and is characterized by persistent disease of more than 2 years’ duration, frequently with interpulmonary involvement and chronic uveitis. Extended corticosteroid therapy may be required. Pulmonary disease is the major cause of morbidity; overall mortality from sarcoidosis approaches 5% but may be as high as 10% with neurosarcoidosis.
Systemic lupus, myasthenia gravis, and Behçet disease do not present with this clinical picture.

Q2912
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is a helpful diagnostic characteristic of multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (shown)?
Correct answer: D. usually unilateral
Rationale
Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome is usually unilateral. It is most common in young females, not males. The tempo of onset is typically rapid or explosive. The associated peripapillary, central, or cecocentral scotomata usually resolve over several weeks. Recurrence is uncommon.

Q2913
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the most appropriate treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii choroiditis?
Correct answer: D. trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole, or pentamidine
Rationale
Patients with AIDS are at greater risk than the general population for P jirovecii pneumonia. In rare cases, this infection can result in choroidal infiltrates that contain the microorganisms. P jirovecii can present as choroiditis that consists of slightly elevated, plaquelike, yellow-white lesions located in the choroid, with minimal vitritis. On fluorescein angiography, these lesions tend to be hypofluorescent in the early phase and hyperfluorescent in the later phases. If disseminated P jirovecii infection is suspected, an extensive examination by an infectious disease specialist is required.
Treatment of P jirovecii choroiditis involves a 3-week regimen of intravenous trimethoprim (20 mg/kg/day) and sulfamethoxazole (100 mg/kg/day) or pentamidine (4 mg/kg/day). Within 3–12 weeks, most of the yellow-white lesions disappear, leaving mild overlying pigmentary changes. Vision is usually not affected.

Q2914
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
Why do autoimmune regulator (AIRE)–deficient mice develop spontaneous uveitis?
Correct answer: C. Autoreactive T cells escape deletion.
Rationale
AIRE is a transcription factor used by the thymus in the process of establishing thymic tolerance. Early in life, the thymus expresses many cell-type–specific proteins; T-cell clones reactive to these proteins are deleted. This mechanism is important in the development of self-tolerance. Mice deficient in AIRE do not express these proteins during development; thus, autoreactive T cells escape deletion, and the mice spontaneously develop a posterior uveitis.

Q2915
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
By what mechanism does cyclosporine treat uveitis?
Correct answer: A. inhibits T-cell receptor signal transduction and downregulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) activity
Rationale
Types of immunomodulatory therapy (IMT), also known as immunosuppressive or disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), are often divided into nonbiologic-IMT and biologic agents. Cyclosporine is a nonbiologic-IMT, and furthermore is a T-cell inhibitor, which is so-called due to its mechanism of action. Cyclosporine inhibits T-cells by inhibiting calcineurin, which then stops T-cell receptor signal transduction (T-cell signaling), and downregulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) activity. IL-2 is downregulated due to decreased IL-2 gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4+ lymphocytes. Tacrolimus is the other T-cell inhibitor or calcineurin inhibitor that is used for uveitis treatment.
The other answers describe mechanisms of action (MOA) of other non-biologic and biologic IMT medications. Beside T-cell inhibitors, nonbiologic-IMT medications also include antimetabolites and alkylating agents. Biologic agents are genetically engineered proteins targeting specific immune processes, and they include tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) inhibitors and inhibitors of others proinflammatory mediators.
The answer choice "inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and DNA replication, and causes extracellular release of adenosine" describes the MOA of methotrexate, which is an antimetabolite. It is a folic acid analogue and dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor. It reduces DNA replication, but the anti-inflammatory mechanism occurs due to extracellular release of adenosine. The other antimetabolites used to treat uveitis include azathioprine, which is a purine nucleoside analogue that interferes with DNA replication and RNA transcription, and mycophenolate mofetil, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and DNA replication.
The answer choice "alkylates purines in DNA and RNA causing abnormal DNA replication and cell death" describes the MOA of cyclophosphamide, which is an alkylating agent. It alkylates purines in DNA and RNA, causing impaired DNA replication and cell death. The other alkylating agent used to treat uveitis is chlorambucil, which also interferes with DNA replication. Cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil are typically reserved for severe, vision-threatening, or life-threatening inflammation that other less toxic therapies failed to manage.
The answer choice "directly inhibits tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) as a fully human monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibody against TNF-α" describes the MOA of the biologic agent adalimumab, which is a TNF-α inhibitor. It is a fully human monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibody that targets TNF-α. It was the first FDA-approved systemic medication for noninfectious uveitis. The other TNF-α inhibitor that is used for uveitis treatment currently is infliximab. It is a mouse/human chimeric immunoglobulin G1 kappa (KgG1κ) monoclonal antibody against TNF-α.
Within the category of biologic agents, besides TNF-α inhibitors, there are also others including rituximab, which is a chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20+ cells (mostly B lymphocytes), interferon alpha-2a/2b (IFN-α2a/2b), which has antiviral, immunomodulatory, and antiangiogenic effects, and abatacept, which inhibits T-cell costimulation.

Q2916
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 54-year-old white woman presents with floaters, photopsia, and nyctalopia of several months' duration. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes, and there are bilateral hypopigmented choroidal lesions and mild vitritis. What blood test is most consistent with the diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. HLA-A29
Rationale
HLA-A29 is associated with birdshot chorioretinopathy in more than 95% of cases, and has a sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 93%. Symptoms include floaters, photopsias, nyctalopia, and decreased contrast sensitivity. The clinical features are characterized by yellow choroidal lesions, vasculitis, and mild vitritis. When the clinical features are suggestive of birdshot, HLA-A29 testing is warranted and, if results are negative, should prompt consideration of another possible etiology or diagnosis. Approximately 7% of the general population will be HLA-A29 positive.
The presence of HLA-B27 is typically evaluated when a patient presents with noninfectious recurrent anterior nongranulomatous uveitis or anterior uveitis that is characterized by hypopyon. The patient will classically be someone with symptoms of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, or inflammatory bowel disease).
HLA-DR14 has been associated with some cases of tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis (TINU) syndrome.
HLA-B51 is associated with some cases of Behçet disease, especially when there is ocular involvement in Behçet disease.

Q2917
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
What is the mechanism by which autoimmune regulator (AIRE)-deficient mice, a murine model of uveitis, develop ocular inflammation?
Correct answer: A. AIRE-deficient mice do not express cell-type-specific proteins and therefore self-reactive T-cells are not deleted.
Rationale
AIRE-deficient mice lack a transcription factor used by the thymus in the development of T-cell self-tolerance. Consequently, T-cells that may be autoreactive are not deleted and can go on to develop autoimmunity against self antigens, including IRBP, thereby causing posterior uveitis. Thus, self-tolerance does not occur in the thymus of AIRE-deficient mice. Non-AIRE-deficient mice are immunized with retinal S-antigen or IRBP-derived peptides to induce experimental autoimmune uveitis (EAU).

Q2918
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
For a patient with intermediate uveitis and a recent tick bite, what is the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)–recommended testing protocol for suspected Lyme disease?
Correct answer: A. enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for Lyme IgM and IgG antibodies followed by Western immunoblot testing
Rationale
Lyme disease is diagnosed on the basis of clinical signs, symptoms, and a history of possible exposure. The US CDC currently recommends a 2-step approach to testing for Lyme antibodies: (1) an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (or rarely, an indirect immunofluorescence assay) and (2) an immunoblot (in this case, a Western blot). Both steps can be done using the same blood specimen. If the assay result is negative, no further testing is necessary. Results are considered positive only if both steps test positive. Performing only the Western blot analysis can increase the false-positive rate. Polymerase chain reaction–based assays can be used to amplify Borrelia burgdorferi DNA found in ocular fluids; however, this assay is rarely performed at present.

Q2919
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
In addition to herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus, what member of the herpesvirus family is most likely to cause unilateral anterior uveitis?
Correct answer: C. cytomegalovirus
Rationale
Viral infections may cause either anterior or posterior uveitis. The most common viruses causing uveitis are cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes zoster, and herpes simplex. CMV is being increasingly recognized in Asian populations as a cause of a chronic, unilateral anterior uveitis associated with elevated intraocular pressure.
Epstein-Barr virus is the viral agent commonly associated with infectious mononucleosis (IM). A mild, self-limiting follicular conjunctivitis, usually appearing early in the course of the disease, is most common with acquired IM. Less frequently reported anterior ocular manifestations of acquired IM include epithelial or stromal keratitis; episcleritis; and bilateral, granulomatous anterior uveitis.
HHV 6 and 7 do not cause uveitis. They cause a febrile illness in children called roseola that is characterized by high temperatures, followed by a rash that does not desquamate.

Q2920
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A 48-year-old woman is referred for glaucoma evaluation. On initial examination, she is found to have intraocular pressure (IOP) of 27 mm Hg OU, corneal pachymetry of 570 OD and 575 OS, and normal results OU from analysis of retinal nerve fiber layer with optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the optic nerve head. What is the best next step in her management, based on findings of the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS)?
Correct answer: A. Obtain standard automated perimetry OU.
Rationale
This patient may be a glaucoma suspect based on potential ocular hypertension from her initial IOP readings. Since her OCT appears within normal limits, indicating likely normal anatomic structure of the ONH, it is important to assess her peripheral vision for any early deficits that may be glaucomatous in nature. Visual field testing, or standard automated perimetry (SAP) is used to assess functional changes. In the OHTS, it was found that a higher pattern standard deviation on visual field testing was an important risk factor for development of POAG. Other important risk factors from the OHTS include older age, higher IOP, thinner corneas, and a larger baseline cup-disc ratio.
Until complete testing, including visual field analysis, can be obtained in this patient, starting medical or surgical therapy is not indicated. It is also important to perform all baseline testing before moving to a longer period for follow-up, such as 1 year.

Q2921
Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation
A Japanese woman presents with bilateral retinal vasculitis and retinitis. She has a history of painful vaginal ulcerative lesions that have never responded to antiviral therapy. What other feature is needed to classify her as having Behçet disease?
Correct answer: D. at least 3 oral aphthous ulcers annually
Rationale
The criteria for Behçet disease are entirely clinical. In addition to having at least 3 oral aphthous ulcers each year, a patient must have 2 of the following: ocular inflammation, recurrent genital ulcers, skin lesions (such as erythema nodosum, folliculitis, or acneiform pustules), and a positive cutaneous pathergy test (per the International Study Group for Behçet Disease). While HLA-B51 positivity has been associated with Behçet disease, this test is not part of the diagnostic criteria. Gingival hyperplasia is not associated with Behçet disease, but can be a side effect of cyclosporine. Periventricular white matter lesions on MRI can be seen in multiple sclerosis.
